252027.title: Devil's Punch Bowl
252027.extract:
The Devil's Punch Bowl is a 282.2-hectare (697-acre) visitor attraction and biological Site of Special Scientific Interest situated just to the east of the village of Hindhead in the English county of Surrey. It is part of the Wealden Heaths Phase II Special Protection Area.
The Punch Bowl is a large natural amphitheatre and is the source of many stories about the area. The London to Portsmouth road (the A3) skirted the rim of the site before the Hindhead Tunnel was built in 2011. The land is owned and maintained by the National Trust as part of the "Hindhead Commons and the Devil's Punch Bowl" property. The highest point of the rim of the bowl is Gibbet Hill, which is 272 metres (892 ft) above sea level and commands a panoramic view that includes, on a clear day, the skyline of London some 38 miles (61 km) away.
The Devil's Punch Bowl was featured on the 2005 TV programme Seven Natural Wonders as one of the wonders of the South.

The '''Devil's Punch Bowl''' is a {{convert| 282.2 |ha|acre|abbr=off|adj=on}} [[visitor attraction]] and biological [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] situated just to the east of the village of [[Hindhead]] in the English county of [[Surrey]]. It is part of the Wealden Heaths Phase II [[Special Protection Area]].<ref name=dsv>{{cite web |url=https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteDetail.aspx?SiteCode=S1000109&SiteName=&countyCode=41&responsiblePerson=&SeaArea=&IFCAArea=  |title=Designated Sites View:  Devil's Punch Bowl |series=Sites of Special Scientific Interest |publisher=Natural England |access-date=7 November 2018 |archive-date=3 January 2019 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190103224807/https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteDetail.aspx?SiteCode=S1000109&SiteName=&countyCode=41&responsiblePerson=&SeaArea=&IFCAArea=}}</ref><ref name=map>{{cite web|url=https://magic.defra.gov.uk/MagicMap.aspx?startTopic=Designations&activelayer=sssiIndex&query=HYPERLINK%3D%271000109%27 |title=Map of Devil's Punch Bowl|series= Sites of Special Scientific Interest|publisher=Natural England|access-date=  7 November 2018}}</ref><ref name=nt>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/hindhead-and-devils-punchbowl|title=Hindhead Commons and the Devil's Punch Bowl|website=National Trust|access-date=16 December 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=  https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteGeneralDetail.aspx?SiteCode=UK9012132&SiteName=&countyCode=41&responsiblePerson=&unitId=&SeaArea=&IFCAArea=|title=  Designated Sites View:   Wealden Heaths Phase II | series= Special Protection Areas |publisher=Natural England|access-date = 7 November 2018}}</ref>

The Punch Bowl is a large natural [[amphitheatre]] and is the source of many stories about the area. The London to [[Portsmouth]] road (the [[A3 road|A3]]) skirted the rim of the site before the [[Hindhead Tunnel]] was built in 2011. The land is owned and maintained by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] as part of the "Hindhead Commons and the Devil's Punch Bowl" property. The highest point of the rim of the bowl is [[Gibbet Hill, Hindhead|Gibbet Hill]], which is {{convert|272|m}} [[Above Ordnance Datum|above sea level]] and commands a panoramic view that includes, on a clear day, the skyline of London some {{convert|38|mi|km}} away.<ref name=nt/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-surrey-14278289 |title=Tunnel vision becomes a reality |first=Nick |last=Tarver |date=27 July 2011 |access-date=16 December 2018 |work=BBC News |publisher=[[BBC]]}}</ref>

The Devil's Punch Bowl was featured on the 2005 TV programme ''[[Seven Natural Wonders]]'' as one of the wonders of the South.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/england/sevenwonders/south/devils_punchbowl/ |title=Seven Man Made Wonders |publisher=[[BBC]] |access-date=20 June 2018}}</ref>

== Toponym ==
[[Image:The old A3 at Hindhead (aerial).jpg|right|thumb|Aerial view of the Devil's Punch Bowl in January 2007, before the closure of the old A3.]]
The name Devil's Punch Bowl dates from at least 1768, the year that [[John Rocque]]'s map of the area was published. This was 18 years before the [[Unknown Sailor|murder of the unknown sailor]] on [[Gibbet Hill, Hindhead|Gibbet Hill]], so this event was clearly not the origin of the name. Prior to 1768, it was marked as "y<sup>e</sup> Bottom" on a map by [[John Ogilby]] dated 1675. The northern end of the Bowl is known as Highcombe Bottom which exists in different variants: Hackombe Bottom, Hacham Bottom, and Hackham Bottom.<ref>John Rocque 1768</ref><ref>Lindley and Crossley 1793</ref><ref>Ordnance Survey 1811</ref>

== Geology ==
This part of Surrey comprises a [[sandstone]] known as the [[Hythe Formation]] that lies above a [[mudstone]] known as the [[Atherfield Clay Formation]]. The bowl's deep depression is believed to be the result of erosion caused by spring water beneath the sandstone, causing the upper level to collapse. The steep slopes are characterised by heathland, streams and woodland.

The site, which has been designated a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]], has abundant wildlife such as the [[lesser spotted woodpecker]] and [[common redstart]]. It has been known for the [[wood warbler]], a rare summer visitor with the last documented sighting in 2009.<ref>{{cite web|title=RSPB: North West Surrey|url=https://ww2.rspb.org.uk/groups/nwsurrey/reports/217386|access-date=7 November 2018}}</ref>

== Roads ==
During the [[Tudor period]] in the 16th century, [[Portsmouth]] developed into a major [[naval dockyard]], needing access to London. The steep gradients of the Devil's Punch Bowl and nearby [[Gibbet Hill, Hindhead|Gibbet Hill]] made this difficult. As a consequence, there have been three phases of road construction through the Devil's Punch Bowl.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.historicdockyard.co.uk/ |title=Welcome to Portsmouth Historic Dockyard |publisher=Portsmouth Historic Dockyard Ltd |access-date=8 August 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110810082525/http://www.historicdockyard.co.uk/ |archive-date=10 August 2011 |url-status=live }}</ref> 

===Earliest route===
[[File: Celtic cross on Gibbet Hill.JPG|left|thumb|A granite Celtic Cross on [[Gibbet Hill, Hindhead|Gibbet Hill]] that commemorates the site of the 1786 murder of the [[Unknown Sailor]]]]
The Old Portsmouth Road is the oldest highway through the area. It is a [[Ridgeway (road)|ridgeway]] that skirts the Punch Bowl to the summit of Gibbet Hill before descending into [[Hindhead]]. The murder of an unknown sailor in 1786 on this route is commemorated by the Sailor's Stone. The route is still used by walkers, cyclists and horse-riders.<ref name=StripMap>{{cite map |url=http://freepages.genealogy.rootsweb.ancestry.com/~genmaps/genfiles/COU_files/ENG/HAM/gentsmag_lon-winchester_rd_1765.html |publisher=[[The Gentleman's Magazine]] |via=ancestry.com |title=A Map of the Roads from London to Portsmouth, Chichester, Southampton, Pool & from Southampton to Winchester |year=1765 |access-date=17 August 2011 |archive-date=3 October 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091003184927/https://freepages.genealogy.rootsweb.ancestry.com/~genmaps/genfiles/COU_files/ENG/HAM/gentsmag_lon-winchester_rd_1765.html}}</ref><ref name=WeyRiver>{{cite web |url=http://www.weyriver.co.uk/theriver/places_10_hindheadtunnel.html |title=The Devil's Punch Bowl and the Hindhead Tunnel |publisher=Weyriver Freelance Community |access-date=5 August 2011 |archive-date=16 August 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110816014825/http://www.weyriver.co.uk/theriver/places_10_hindheadtunnel.html}}</ref>

===Turnpike===
[[File:Devil's Punch Bowl, old A3 closed to traffic 1.jpg|thumb|The 1826 route was created by a [[Cut (earthworks)|cutting]] through hillside of the Devil's Punch Bowl]]
In 1748 [[Kingston-Upon-Thames]] to Sheet Bridge [[Turnpike trust|Turnpike Company]] took over the management of Old Portsmouth Road. They installed mileposts, toll houses, gates and maintained the highway through the Devil's Punch Bowl. However, by the early 19th century increased pedestrian and horse-drawn traffic meant this steep section of highway between Portsmouth and London required major improvements.

In 1826, the Portsmouth & Sheet Bridge Turnpike Road Trust began asking for tenders from bidders to improve the road. The winning bid resulted in a completely new highway through the Devil's Punch Bowl. Old Portmouth Road was abandoned in favour of a new [[Cut (earthworks)|cutting]] {{convert|200|ft|abbr=on}} below the ridgeline. By digging into the hillside at a lower height, the new road removed the steep ascents and descents of the summit over Gibbet Hill. The surveyed route had a gradient of no more than 5% which meant larger and heavier horse-drawn carriages could now use this section of the road. 

In the 1920s, this route became the [[A3 road (Great Britain)|A3]] when road numbering was introduced by the [[Ministry of Transport (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Transport]] with the advent of motorised transport. For almost hundred years, it remained a principal route from London to Portsmouth.<ref name=NtHistory>{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/surrey/hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punch-bowl/the-history-of-hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punchbowl |title=The History of Hindhead Commons and the Devil’s Punch Bowl |publisher=[[National Trust]] |access-date=13 December 2024 |archive-date=13 December 2024 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241213181033/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/surrey/hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punch-bowl/the-history-of-hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punchbowl}}</ref>

=== Return to nature ===
[[File:Old A3 Hindhead.JPG|thumb|right|The 1826 [[turnpike trust|turnpike]] route of the former A3 has been removed.]]
By the start of the 21st century most of the A3 had become a [[dual carriageway]], leaving only the section through Hindhead and the Devil's Punch Bowl as [[single carriageway]]. Due to daily traffic volumes, this section operated at or above capacity for much of the day and had an accident rate 40% higher than the national average for that class of road. As a consequence, the decision to bypass the route over the Devil's Punch Bowl was taken.

The [[Hindhead Tunnel]], which passes directly under Gibbet Hill and the Punch Bowl, opened in 2011. The 1826 turnpike route of the former A3 was completely removed with the intention that it will revert to natural heathland.<ref name=Mottmac/><ref name=HaHindhead/><ref name=NtWork/><ref name=PublicInquiry>{{cite web |url=http://www.godalmingcycle.org.uk/docs/Hindhead_report.pdf |title=Report to the First Secretary of State and the Secretaries of State for Transport and for Environment Food and Rural Affairs; File Reference: HA/061/002/0002 |first1=Alan |last1=Gray |first2=John |last2=Watson |publisher=The Planning Inspectorate |date=24 August 2005 |access-date=6 August 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100120052717/http://www.godalmingcycle.org.uk/docs/Hindhead_report.pdf |archive-date=20 January 2010 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Conservation ==
[[File:Devil's Punch Bowl National Trust sign, Hindhead (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|National Trust sign at the Punch Bowl]]
The Devil's Punch Bowl, along with Hindhead Common, was acquired by the [[National Trust]] in 1906, making it one of the first open spaces acquired by the Trust. The beauty of the area and the diversity of nature it attracts resulted in the Devil's Punch Bowl being designated as a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] on 30 April 1986.<ref name=dsv/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://blackdownhindheadntsupporters.org/locations/the-devils-punch-bowl-hindhead-common/ |title=The Devil's Punch Bowl & Hindhead Common |publisher=Black Down and Hindhead Supporters of the National Trust |access-date=14 December 2024}}</ref> 

This ownership and status helped save the Devil's Punch Bowl from above-ground redevelopment of the [[A3 road|A3]] in the first decade of the 21st century. The National Trust co-operated with developers [[Balfour Beatty]], who designed the alternative [[Hindhead Tunnel]], running underneath the area. The tunnel preserves not only the area from the road widening originally proposed but also removes the heavy traffic congestion which previously affected this section of the A3 in peak hours.<ref name=Mottmac>{{cite web |url=http://www.tunnels.mottmac.com/projects/?mode=type&id=3402 |title=A3 Hindhead tunnel |publisher=Mott MacDonald |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070504015651/http://www.tunnels.mottmac.com/projects/?mode=type&id=3402 |archive-date=2007-05-04 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=HaHindhead>{{cite web |url=http://www.highways.gov.uk/roads/projects/3832.aspx |publisher=Highways Agency |title=A3 Hindhead Improvement |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070629031024/http://www.highways.gov.uk/roads/projects/3832.aspx |archive-date=2007-06-29 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=NtWork>{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/surrey/hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punch-bowl/our-work-at-hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punch-bowl |title=Our work at Hindhead Commons and the Devil’s Punch Bowl |publisher=[[National Trust]] |access-date=13 December 2024 |archive-date=13 December 2024 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241213181733/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/surrey/hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punch-bowl/our-work-at-hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punch-bowl}}</ref>

The National Trust provide car parking and a cafe at the Hindhead end of the Devil's Punch Bowl. A number of different footpaths, of differing length and difficulty, provide access to all parts of the Punch Bowl and surrounding area.<ref name=nt/><ref name=NtWalk>{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/surrey/hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punch-bowl/walking-at-hindhead-commons |title=Walking at Hindhead Commons and the Devil's Punch Bowl |publisher=[[National Trust]] |access-date=14 December 2024 |archive-date=14 December 2024 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241214175100/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/surrey/hindhead-commons-and-the-devils-punch-bowl/walking-at-hindhead-commons}}</ref>

The Hindhead [[youth hostel]], run by the [[Youth Hostels Association (England & Wales)|Youth Hostel Association]], used to be located inside the bowl but closed in 2015.<ref>{{cite news |title=Popular youth hostel closing down |url=https://www.farnhamherald.com/news/popular-youth-hostel-closing-down-168074 |work=Farnham Herald |date=10 November 2014 |access-date=14 December 2024 |archive-date=14 December 2024 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241214175651/https://www.farnhamherald.com/news/popular-youth-hostel-closing-down-168074}}</ref>

== In fiction ==
Punch Bowl Farm, at the northern end of the Devil's Punch Bowl, was the home of children's novelist [[Monica Edwards]] from 1947 until 1998. In her books she renamed the farm Punchbowl Farm.<ref>{{cite newspaper The Times |title= Monica Edwards |date= 7 February 1998 |issue= 66119 |page= 25 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Tucker |first=Nicholas |title=Obituary: Monica Edwards |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/obituary-monica-edwards-1144457.html |access-date=9 November 2019 |work=[[The Independent]] |date=13 February 1998}}</ref> In [[Charles Dickens]]' novel ''[[Nicholas Nickleby]]'', Nicholas and Smike visit the Devil's Punch Bowl on their journey to [[Portsmouth]].<ref>{{cite book |last= Dickens |first= Charles |author-link= Charles Dickens |year= 1839 |title= The life and adventures of Nicholas Nickleby |publisher= Chapman and Hall |location= London |url= https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nicholas_Nickleby |access-date= 10 February 2023 |page= 207}}</ref>

The third novel in the [[Horatio Hornblower]] series, ''[[Flying Colours (novel)|Flying Colours]]'' by [[C.S. Forester]], makes a one-line reference to the Devil's Punch Bowl in chapter eighteen as Hornblower is returning to London: "Even the marvellous beauty of the Devil's Punch Bowl was lost on Hornblower as they drove past it."<ref>{{cite book |last= Forester |first= C. S. |author-link= C. S. Forester |year= 1951 |orig-year= 1938 |title= [[Flying Colours (novel)|Flying Colours]] |publisher= Michael Joseph |location= London |chapter= XVIII |page= 188 }}</ref>

[[File:Devil's Punch Bowl, Hindhead Common - Christopher-Hilton.jpg|thumb|right|The Devil's Punch Bowl seen from above, by the Sailor's Stone]]
The "Devil's Punch-Bowl in Surrey" is briefly mentioned in ''The Shining Pyramid'', a short story by [[Arthur Machen]],<ref>{{cite book |last= Machen |first= Arthur |year= 1923 |title= The Shining Pyramid |publisher= Starett, Vincent |url= https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Shining_Pyramid_(collection)/The_Shining_Pyramid |access-date= 10 February 2023 |at= Chapter 5: The Little People }}</ref> and in "The Manhood of Edward Robinson", the fifth story in [[Agatha Christie]]'s ''The Listerdale Mystery and Other Stories''.<ref>{{cite book |last= Christie |first= Agatha |author-link= Agatha Christie |year= 2016 |orig-year= 1934 |title= The Listerdale Mystery and other stories |publisher= Harper Collins |location= London |isbn= 978-0-00-819643-1 |pages=112–113}}</ref> The area is the setting for [[Sabine Baring-Gould]]'s novel ''The Broom-squire''.<ref>{{cite book |last= Baring-Gould |first= S. |year= 1895 |title= The Broom-squire |publisher= Frederick A. Stokes |location= London }}</ref>

== Local legends ==
According to a local legend the [[Devil]] hurled lumps of earth at the god [[Thor]] to annoy him. The hollow out of which he scooped the earth became the Punch Bowl. The local village of [[Thursley]] means Thor's place.<ref>The Concise Oxford Dictionary of English Place-names – Fourth Edition 1977 – page 472</ref> An alternative version of this story says that Thor threw the lumps of earth at the Devil, who was annoying Thor by jumping across the [[Devil's Jumps, Churt|Devil's Jumps]].<ref>{{cite news |last= Phillips |first = Jamie |date= 6 June 2020 |title= The mythical battle between Thor and the Devil said to have created Surrey beauty spot |work= Surrey Live |url= https://www.getsurrey.co.uk/news/surrey-news/mythical-battle-between-thor-devil-18369732 |access-date= 10 February 2023 }}</ref>

==Legacy project==
[[File:Portal (2013) public sculpture at Hindhead National Trust situated on former A3 road; view North.JPG|thumb|right|'Portal' sculpture at Devil's Punch Bowl]]
A lottery award from the [[Heritage Lottery Fund]] was made in 2012 for a project with young people from schools in the area, celebrating the landscape. Several sculptures marked the completion in early 2013 and a carving from a 3-tonne block of [[Portland stone]] by [[Jon Edgar]] now sits on the spine of the former A3 near the visitor centre.<ref name=nt/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cultureshift.org.uk/news/heritage-lottery-funding-for-hindhead-a3d-legacy-project/|title=Culture Shift » Heritage Lottery funding for Hindhead A3D legacy project|website=www.cultureshift.org.uk|access-date=16 December 2018}}</ref>

468180.title: Box Hill, Surrey
468180.extract:
Box Hill is a summit of the North Downs in Surrey, approximately 31 km (19 mi) south-west of London. It is named after the ancient box woodland found on the steepest west-facing chalk slopes overlooking the River Mole. The western part of the hill is owned and managed by the National Trust, whilst the village of Box Hill lies on higher ground to the east. The highest point is Betchworth Clump at 224 m (735 ft) above OD, although the Salomons Memorial (at 172 metres) overlooking the town of Dorking is the most popular viewpoint.
Box Hill is part of the Surrey Hills National Landscape and forms part of the Mole Gap to Reigate Escarpment Site of Special Scientific Interest.  The north- and south-facing slopes support an area of chalk downland, noted for its orchids and other rare plant species. The hill provides a habitat for 38 species of butterfly, and has given its name to a species of squash bug, now found throughout south-east England.
An estimated 850,000 people visit Box Hill each year. The National Trust visitors' centre provides both a cafeteria and gift shop, and panoramic views of the western Weald may be enjoyed from the North Downs Way, a long-distance footpath that runs along the south-facing scarp slope.  Box Hill featured prominently on the route of the 2012 Summer Olympics cycling road race events.

The north- and south-facing slopes support an area of chalk downland, noted for its orchids and other rare plant species.{{cite web |url= http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-great_days_out/w-nature-places_to_visit/w-nature-places_to_visit-boxhill.htm |title= Box Hill |author= Oates M |year= 2008 |work= Places to Visit for Wildlife |publisher= National Trust |access-date= 3 April 2011 |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110517040554/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-great_days_out/w-nature-places_to_visit/w-nature-places_to_visit-boxhill.htm |archive-date= 17 May 2011 |df= dmy-all }} The hill provides a habitat for 38 species of butterfly,{{cite web |url= https://butterfly-conservation.org/sites/default/files/56-autumn-2013.pdf |title= News from Box Hill |last= Jeffcoate |first= Gail |year= 2013 |website= Surrey Skipper |publisher= Butterfly Conservation |access-date= 25 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191025152923/https://butterfly-conservation.org/sites/default/files/56-autumn-2013.pdf |archive-date= 25 October 2019 |url-status= live }} and has given its name to a species of [[Coreidae|squash bug]], now found throughout south-east England.{{cite web |url= http://www.britishbugs.org.uk/heteroptera/Coreidae/gonocerus_acuteangulatus.html |title= ''Gonocerus acuteangulatus'' Box Bug |author= Bantock T and Botting J |year= 2010 |work= British Bugs: An online identification guide to UK Hemiptera |publisher= britishbugs.org.uk |access-date= 29 March 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090615042004/http://www.britishbugs.org.uk/heteroptera/Coreidae/gonocerus_acuteangulatus.html |archive-date= 15 June 2009 |url-status= live }} An estimated 850,000 people visit Box Hill each year. The National Trust visitors' centre provides both a cafeteria and gift shop, and [[panorama|panoramic]] views of the western Weald may be enjoyed from the [[North Downs Way]], a long-distance footpath that runs along the south-facing [[escarpment|scarp slope]]. Box Hill featured prominently on the route of the [[Cycling at the 2012 Summer Olympics|2012 Summer Olympics cycling]] road race events.{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/interactive/2011/feb/10/olympics-2012-cycling-road-race-route |title=Olympics 2012: cycling road race route |work=Guardian |date=11 February 2011 |format=Adobe Flash |access-date=18 February 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307225132/http://www.theguardian.com/sport/interactive/2011/feb/10/olympics-2012-cycling-road-race-route |archive-date=7 March 2016 |url-status=live }} {{TOC limit|3}} ==Geography== Box Hill, approximately {{convert|31|km|mi|abbr=on}} south-west of central London, stands at the south-eastern corner of the Mole Gap, the valley carved by the River Mole through the North Downs.{{harvnb|Bannister|1999|p=2}} Its summit, {{convert|224|m|ft}} above [[Ordnance Datum]], is the 12th highest in Surrey.[http://www.hills-database.co.uk/downloads.html Database of British and Irish Hills] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180805042151/http://www.hills-database.co.uk/downloads.html |date=5 August 2018 }} Retrieved 6 March 2015 The western boundary of the hill is defined by the River Mole, which has cut a steep [[cliff]], exposing the chalk bedrock.{{harvnb|Hutchings|Bridges|Sankey|1969|p=9}} The [[Vale of Holmesdale]] lies immediately to the south, below the scarp slope. The northern and eastern boundaries are defined by [[dry valley|dry river valleys]], which were created during the [[last glacial period|last Ice Age]]. The total area of the hill is approximately {{convert|11|km2|sqmi}}, of which half is owned by the National Trust. ==The village== {{Infobox UK place |static_image_name=File:St Andrew's Church, Box Hill (Geograph Image 2266120 e41e2a89).jpg |static_image_caption=St Andrew's Church, Box Hill village |country = England |coordinates = |official_name= Box Hill |map_type= |label_position= |population =1,320 |population_ref=(2019 estimate){{cite web |url=https://www.citypopulation.de/en/uk/southeastengland/surrey/E34004309__box_hill/ |title=City Population Estimate 2019-06-30 |last= |first= |date=30 October 2020 |website=City Population.de |publisher= |access-date=24 January 2021 |archive-date=12 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190712040625/http://citypopulation.de/en/uk/southeastengland/surrey/E34004309__box_hill/ |url-status=live }} |civil_parish=n/a |shire_district= [[Mole Valley]] |shire_county = [[Surrey]] |region= South East England |constituency_westminster= [[Dorking and Horley (UK Parliament constituency)|Dorking and Horley]] |post_town= Tadworth |postcode_district = KT20 |postcode_area= KT |dial_code= 01306 / 01737 }} The village of Box Hill is to the east of the summit and to the west of the Country Park owned by the National Trust. The earliest flint cottages date from the 1800s, although much of the village was constructed in the first half of the 20th century.{{harvnb|Mountford|1974|pp=3–4}} By 2005 there were more than 800 dwellings, of which over five hundred were mobile homes. An estimated 41% of the community is aged 60 or over.{{cite web |url= http://www.connectedsurrey.com/stylesheet.asp?file=17032006112104 |title= Box Hill Project |author= Fry R |year= 2006 |work= Community Case Studies |publisher= The Connected Surrey Partnership |access-date= 13 April 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120425090813/http://www.connectedsurrey.com/stylesheet.asp?file=17032006112104 |archive-date= 25 April 2012 |url-status= live }} St Andrew's Church, part of the [[ecclesiastical parish]] of Headley, was consecrated in 1969 and the village hall opened in 1974.{{cite web |url=http://myweb.tiscali.co.uk/friendsofstandrewsbh/history_part_1.htm |title=History |author=Langley D |year=2000 |work=The Church on the Hill |publisher=Friends of St Andrews Box Hill |access-date=24 July 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004213848/http://myweb.tiscali.co.uk/friendsofstandrewsbh/history_part_1.htm |archive-date=4 October 2013 |url-status=dead }}{{harvnb|Mountford|1974|p=3}} The village is not part of a civil parish. ==History== ===Early history=== [[File:Beech pollard - live }} ===Medieval and early modern periods=== The [[Warren (burrow)|pillow mounds]] to the north-east of the Salomons Memorial are thought to date from the medieval period and were probably constructed as artificial [[Warren (burrow)|warrens]] for rabbits. High Ashurst warren is recorded as remaining in use until the late 18th century.{{harvnb|Bannister|1999|p=20}} A second warren was probably situated close to Warren Farm in the Headley Valley and it has been speculated that the present farmhouse was originally the warrener's cottage. [[File:Boxhill surrey trees.jpg|thumb|right|Box and yew trees growing on the steep, western slope of Box Hill, above the River Mole.]] The origin of the [[buxus|box trees]] growing on the hill is disputed. Several sources from the late 18th century suggest that they were planted by [[Thomas Howard, 21st Earl of Arundel]] during the reign of [[Charles I of England|Charles I]].{{sfn|Beavan|1777|p=2}} However Howard never owned the Box Hill estate{{harvnb|Littledale|Locock|Sankey|1984|p=12}} and older medieval documents make reference to local individuals with surnames including ''Atteboxe'', ''de la Boxe'' and ''Buxeto'', suggesting that the trees were already common in the area by the 13th century.{{harvnb|Brayley|Britton|1841|p=461}} The diarist [[John Evelyn]] records a visit to the hill in August 1655 to view "those natural bowers, cabinets and shady walks in the box copses".{{harvnb|Evelyn|1870|p=295}} The [[wood grain|close grain]] of the box wood made it highly prized for its [[lumber|timber]] for carving and there are numerous accounts of the sale of trees from the hill throughout the 17th and 18th centuries.{{harvnb|Littledale|Locock|Sankey|1984|p=13}} At the end of the eighteenth century, imports from Portugal reduced the market value of box wood and commercial exploitation of timber from Box Hill appears to have ended with a final sale in 1797. ===Agriculture=== Despite the commercial importance of timber in the [[early modern period]], the woodland on Box Hill was much less extensive at the start of the 19th century than at the start of the 21st. The 1801 [[Betchworth]] Estate Map shows that there was a network of irregularly shaped fields on the top of the hill, where the more fertile [[clay-with-flints]] overlays the chalk. These ‘clearings’ (each up to {{convert|1|ha}}) were cultivated for [[arable land|arable crops]], but by the 1830s [[British Agricultural Revolution|changes in farming practices]] meant that they were too small to be worked economically and many were over-planted with [[beech]] (with some [[oak]]). These deciduous plantations may be distinguished from older yew- and box-dominated woodland on the hill by the uniform age of the trees.{{harvnb|Hutchings|Bridges|Sankey|1969|pp=19–20}}{{harvnb|Littledale|Locock|Sankey|1984|p=14}} Remnants of a few of these arable fields still exist, notably at the head of Juniper Bottom and around the old Box Hill Fort and Swiss Cottage. The Donkey Green (immediately north of the Salomons Memorial) was used as a cricket ground in the 1850s. It acquired its current name in [[Edwardian era|Edwardian times]], when [[donkey rides]] were offered to younger day trippers, although this practice had ceased by [[World War II]].{{harvnb|Tuson|2013|p=7}} The soil covering the north- and south-facing chalk slopes of the hill is too thin and insufficiently fertile to allow cultivation. These areas are indicated as ''sheep-walk'' on the 1801 map and were used as [[pasture]], especially during the winter months when lower ground was too wet for productive grazing. [[Conservation grazing|Grazing]] of these slopes has continued into the 21st century and a herd of [[Belted Galloway]] cattle is used by both Surrey Wildlife Trust and the National Trust to control growth of grasses, thereby allowing wild flowers (including orchids) to flourish.{{cite web |url= https://www.surreywildlifetrust.org/what-we-do/restoring-surreys-nature/conservation-grazing |title= Conservation grazing |author= |website= Surrey Wildlife Trust |access-date= 25 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191023183638/https://www.surreywildlifetrust.org/what-we-do/restoring-surreys-nature/conservation-grazing |archive-date= 23 October 2019 |url-status= live }}{{cite web |url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/conservation-grazing |title= Conservation grazing |author= |website= National Trust |access-date= 25 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191025110156/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/conservation-grazing |archive-date= 25 October 2019 |url-status= live }} [[File:Gorse on Headley Heath, Surrey (Geograph 5380966).jpg|right|thumb|[[Ulex europaeus|Common gorse]] in bloom on Headley Heath.]] Throughout its history, Headley Heath has been used for grazing and local villagers have collected [[Calluna|heather]], [[Ulex europaeus|gorse]] and [[sod|turf]] for bedding and making fires. Although most [[Common land|Rights of Common]] connected with the heath were [[Commons Registration Act 1965|abolished by Act of Parliament in 1965]], the inhabitants of one nearby cottage still have the right to graze [[goose|geese]].{{cite web |url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/headley-heath/features/lords-of-the-manor-and-headley-heath |title= Lords of the manor and Headley Heath |last= Denyer |first= Peter |year= 2015 |publisher= National Trust |access-date= 18 July 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200718164352/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/headley-heath/features/lords-of-the-manor-and-headley-heath |archive-date= 18 July 2020 |url-status= live }} ===Ownership and public access=== The hill was purchased by [[Thomas Hope (banker, born 1769)|Thomas Hope]], shortly before his death in 1831. (Hope was the owner of [[Deepdene House and Gardens|The Deepdene]], the mansion to the east of [[Dorking]].) The [[Mickleham, Surrey|Mickleham Parish]] Records credit Hope's widow, Louisa de la Poer Beresford (whom he had married six years previously), with allowing "free access to the beauties of this hill", however day-trippers had been arriving in significant numbers for more than a century before that.{{cite book |last= Macky |first= John |year= 1714 |volume= 1 |title= A journey through England. In familiar letters. From a gentleman here, to his friend abroad |location= London |publisher= J. Hooke |author-link= John Macky}} Developments in local transport infrastructure over the course of the 18th and 19th centuries, enabled increasing numbers to visit the area. Following the completion of the [[turnpike trust|turnpike road]] between [[Leatherhead]] and [[Dorking]] in 1750, [[stagecoach]]es stopped regularly at the [[Burford Bridge Hotel]].{{harvnb|Shepperd|1991|p=128}} As late as 1879, a daily coach ran non-stop to Box Hill from [[Piccadilly]] with a journey time of 2.5 hours.{{cite news |author= |title= The Boxhill Coach |work= Daily News |location= London |date= 31 March 1879}}{{refn|In March 1879 the coach left Piccadilly at 10:30am every day, arriving at the Burford Bridge Hotel at 1pm. The return journey left Box Hill at 4pm, arriving back in London at 6:30pm.|group=note}} The [[South Eastern Railway (England)|South Eastern Railway]] opened [[Dorking West railway station|the first railway station in Dorking]] in 1849, followed by the [[London, Brighton and South Coast Railway]] (LBSCR), which opened [[Box Hill & Westhumble railway station|the station in the village of Westhumble]] in 1867.{{harvnb|Shepperd|1991|pp=150–151}}{{harvnb|Shepperd|1991|p=137}} The LBSCR ran dedicated excursion trains to Box Hill on Bank Holiday weekends and over 1300 day-trippers were recorded arriving at Westhumble station on 6 August 1883.{{cite news |author= |title= The Bank Holiday |work= The Times |location= London |date= 7 August 1883}} [[File:Box Hill Salomons Memorial 2.jpg|right|thumb|The Salomons Memorial commemorates the gift of {{convert|95|ha|acre|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} of land on Box Hill to the National Trust in 1914.{{refn|Salomons died in September 1915, just over a year after donating the land on Box Hill to the National Trust. His widow opened the Memorial at the viewpoint in August 1920.{{cite newspaper The Times |title= Memorial To Donor Of Box Hill |date= 17 August 1920 |page= 7 |issue= 42491 }}{{cite news |last= Edwards |first= Mark |date= 11 September 2014 |title= Box Hill viewing point reopens to mark 100th anniversary |url= https://www.getsurrey.co.uk/news/nostalgia/box-hill-viewing-point-reopens-7756789 |work= Surrey Live |access-date= 21 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191021083357/https://www.getsurrey.co.uk/news/nostalgia/box-hill-viewing-point-reopens-7756789 |archive-date= 21 October 2019 |url-status= live }}|group=note}}]] The proposals for a [[land value tax]] outlined by Chancellor [[David Lloyd George]] in his [[People's Budget]] of 1909 prompted the trustees of the Deepdene estate to start to sell the unimproved land on the western side of Box Hill.{{harvnb|Littledale|Locock|Sankey|1984|p=15}} As a result of negotiations led by [[Robert Hunter (National Trust)|Sir Robert Hunter]], [[Leopold Salomons]] of [[Norbury Park]] purchased {{convert|95|ha|acre|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} of Box Hill in 1913 for £16,000. The following year, Salomons donated the land, which included the Old Fort, Swiss Cottage and the western flank of the hill above the River Mole, to the National Trust.{{harvnb|Littledale|Locock|Sankey|1984|pp=15–16}} Two further purchases of {{convert|28|ha|acre|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} and {{convert|102|ha|acre|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} transferred Lodge Hill and Ashurst Rough to National Trust ownership in 1921 and 1923.{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/servlet/file/store5/item724521/version1/nt_acquisitions_dec2011-2.pdf |title=National Trust Acquisition Data |year=2010 |publisher=National Trust |access-date=12 February 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120603070439/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/servlet/file/store5/item724521/version1/nt_acquisitions_dec2011-2.pdf |archive-date=3 June 2012}} Following World War II, National Trust acquired Headley Heath, a geologically distinct area of heathland which lies to the north-east of Box Hill village, the majority of which was given as a single donation in 1946.{{refn|In 1946 Mr and Mrs Crookenden gave {{convert|195|ha|acre}} of Headley Heath (and the Lordship of the Manor of Headley) to the National Trust. The family of Lady Warburg donated the {{convert|9|ha|acre|adj=on}} Heath Plantation following her death in 1952.|group=note}} The Trust continued to purchase land, and by the mid-1980s the estate comprised some {{convert|500|ha|acre|abbr=on|sigfig=2}}. The most recent additions to the Box Hill Estate include farmland at Westhumble and at the foot of the hill, purchased in the late 1990s. ===Military history=== [[File:Box Hill Fort.JPG|thumb|Box Hill Fort, constructed in 1899. Note the earth [[blast wall|blast bank]] (left) which protects the south west face of the flat-roofed main building (right).{{National Heritage List for England|num=1018074}}]] In the latter half of the 19th century, growing public concern over the ability of the British armed forces to repel an invasion (stoked, in part, by the serialisation of [[George Tomkyns Chesney|George Tomkyns Chesney's]] 1871 novella [[The Battle of Dorking]]{{harvnb|Tuson|2013|pp=20–21}}), prompted the government to announce the construction of thirteen fortified mobilisation centres, collectively known as the [[London Defence Positions]].{{cite web |url= http://www.waymarking.com/waymarks/WMGCY |title= Box Hill Fort |year= 2006 |work= Historic Forts on Waymarking.com |publisher= waymarking.com |access-date= 10 February 2012 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110806004242/http://www.waymarking.com/waymarks/WMGCY |archive-date= 6 August 2011 |url-status= live }}{{refn|A common misconception is that the forts were built to protect against invasion by the French Emperor [[Napoleon]], however he had died in 1821, almost 80 years before construction began.
The aftermath of the [[Franco-Prussian War]] of 1870 (which led to the [[unification of Germany]]), the reform of the Russian Army following the Crimean War and colonial disputes with France, prompted British fears of a war against an alliance of the main European powers. Lobbying by [[Edward Bruce Hamley|Sir Edward Hamley MP]]{{cite Hansard|house=House of Commons |title= Defences of the Empire - Coast defences of Great Britain |url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1887/mar/14/observations#S3V0312P0_18870314_HOC_240 |date= 14 March 1887 |volume 312 |column_start=238 |column_end=325}} resulted in the Secretary of State for War, [[Edward Stanhope]], presenting the bill for construction of the London Defence Positions to Parliament in 1889.{{harvnb|Beanse|Gill|2011|pp=4–6}}|group=note}} Two centres were built on Box Hill, approximately {{convert|2.5|km|mi|abbr=on}} apart: one close to the present National Trust visitor centre (commonly called Box Hill Fort){{harvnb|Beanse|Gill|2011|pp=17–19}}{{refn|The [[bridle path]] that leads from the bottom of the Burford Spur to the National Trust café, is generally known as the ‘Old Military Road’. Although it is mistakenly believed to have been constructed at the same time as Box Hill Fort, it is visible on the 1869 Ordnance survey map and may pre-date the Zig Zag Road.{{harvnb|Littledale|Locock|Sankey|1984|p=24}}|group=note}} and the other close to the summit of the hill, to the south of the present day Box Hill village (known as Betchworth Fort).{{harvnb|Beanse|Gill|2011|pp=14–16}} The sites were purchased from the trustees of the Hope estate by the [[Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Defence]] in 1891, and construction began in 1899. The two centres were laid out in the form of [[redoubt|infantry redoubts]] typical of the period, but also included [[magazine (artillery)|magazines]] (partially below ground level) for the storage of [[Shell (projectile)|shells]] and [[Cartridge (firearms)|cartridges]].{{harvnb|Littledale|Locock|Sankey|1984|p=23}} (In common with the majority of the eleven other mobilisation centres, the forts were designed for the use of the infantry only and the stored ammunition was intended for the use of [[Field artillery|mobile field artillery]] which would be deployed nearby as required.) The main flat-roofed buildings were built in brick and reinforced concrete and were protected from [[artillery]] fire by crescent-shaped earth blast banks, surrounded by an outer ditch. A [[Haldane reforms|reform of defence policy]] by the Secretary of War [[Richard Haldane, 1st Viscount Haldane|Viscount Haldane]] in 1905 resulted in all 13 centres being declared redundant, and both forts were sold back to the estate trustees in 1908.{{harvnb|Bannister|1999|p=27}} Both forts are protected by a Scheduled Monument listing.{{National Heritage List for England|num=1020370}} The National Trust owns the Box Hill Fort and a metal grill has been placed over the entrance to allow bats to access to their roosts. The Betchworth Fort is in private ownership and is not accessible to the public. [[File:Pill Box - geograph.org.uk - 657135.jpg|thumb|[[Pillbox (military)|Pillbox]] on the south-facing scarp slope of Box Hill (to the north of [[Betchworth Castle]]).]] During World War II, the River Mole comprised part of the fortified [[GHQ Line|GHQ Line B]]. This defensive line ran along the North Downs from [[Farnham]] via [[Guildford]] to Dorking, before following the river to [[Horley]].{{cite web |url= http://ads.ahds.ac.uk/catalogue//adsdata/arch-455-1/dissemination/pdf/Text_Reports/DA12_TEXT_-_DORKING_GAP.pdf |title= Defence Area 12: Dorking Gap |author= Foot W |year= 2009 |work= Defence Areas: a national study of Second World War anti-invasion landscapes in England |publisher= English Heritage |access-date= 11 December 2010 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110811042351/http://ads.ahds.ac.uk/catalogue//adsdata/arch-455-1/dissemination/pdf/Text_Reports/DA12_TEXT_-_DORKING_GAP.pdf |archive-date= 11 August 2011 |url-status= live }} Between Betchworth and Box Hill, the north bank of the River Mole was stabilised and made steeper to prevent wheeled vehicles from crossing. At Boxhill Farm, where access to the river from the north bank was required for the herd of dairy cows, a row of twelve concrete cylinders were cast as an anti-tank measure. Gun mounts were also installed to protect both Boxhill and Deepdene bridges and several [[Pillbox (military)|pillboxes]] were constructed.{{cite journal |author= Marchington T |year= 2000 |title= Wartime Defences: A Second Look |journal= Proceedings of the Leatherhead and District Local History Society |volume= 6 |issue= 4 |pages= 96–100 |publisher= Leatherhead and District Local History Society}}{{cite journal |date=2 March 2011 |title=Box Hill, Surrey: walk of the week |journal=Daily Telegraph |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/activityandadventure/walkingholidays/8356605/Box-Hill-Surrey-walk-of-the-week.html |access-date=29 March 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110309211404/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/activityandadventure/walkingholidays/8356605/Box-Hill-Surrey-walk-of-the-week.html |archive-date=9 March 2011 |url-status=live }} The Stepping Stones at the foot of the hill were removed as an anti-invasion measure. [[Betchworth Quarry and Lime Kilns|Betchworth Quarry]] was used by the British Army in early 1944, to test the firing capabilities of [[Churchill tank]]s.{{harvnb|Chapman|Young|1979|p=154}} ==Geology== ===Rock types=== [[File:Chalk_Face,_Betchworth_Quarry,_Box_Hill,_Surrey.jpg|thumb|The exposed chalk workings of the former Betchworth Quarry on the south-facing scarp slope of Box Hill.{{refn|Note the transmitter mast in the top-left corner of the photograph which, together with the adjacent water tower (not visible in the picture), marks the true summit of Box Hill at {{convert|224|m|ft|abbr=on}} above OD.|group=note}}]] The [[Chalk Group|chalk]] which comprises the majority of Box Hill (and the rest of the [[North Downs]]), has its origins in the late [[Cretaceous]] (approximately 100 – 66 million years ago). For the entirety of this period, south east England was covered by a warm, shallow sea in which [[coccolithophores]], single-celled [[alga]]e with small [[calcite]] skeletons, thrived. As the phytoplankton died, their calcium-rich shells were deposited on the sea bed and, over time, formed the chalk we know today.{{cite journal |vauthors= Hancock JM |year=1975 |title= The petrology of the chalk |journal= Proc. Geol. Assoc. |volume= 86 |issue= 4 |pages= 499–535 |doi= 10.1016/S0016-7878(75)80061-7|bibcode=1975PrGA...86..499H }} Overlying the chalk across much of the higher ground on the hill, is a deposit of [[clay-with-flints]]. Although the origins of this layer are uncertain, the clay is thought to have been formed during several periods of glaciation and was produced by [[cryoturbation]] and decalcification of the chalk.{{cite journal |last1=Gallois |first1= RW |title= The origin of the Clay-with-flints: the missing link|journal=Geoscience in South-West England|date=2009|volume=12|pages=153–161}} This hypothesis is supported by the presence of flint, which is also found in the underlying strata.{{cite web|last1=Anon|title=Clay-with Flints formation|url=http://www.bgs.ac.uk/lexicon/lexicon.cfm?pub=CWF|website=The BGS Lexicon of Named Rock Units|publisher=BGS|access-date=3 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170909085950/http://www.bgs.ac.uk/lexicon/lexicon.cfm?pub=CWF|archive-date=9 September 2017|url-status=live}} The sandy deposits on Headley Heath have their origin in the [[Quaternary]]. The sand and gravels found in this area, indicate the presence of the sea shore.{{harvnb|Chapman|Young|1979|p=26}} On Headley Heath, these deposits are thin and the chalk also comes to the surface in several places, allowing [[calcifuge|acid-loving plants]] to thrive alongside those that [[calcicole|prefer alkaline conditions]], producing the rare [[chalk heath]] habitat. ===Wealden uplift and erosion of the North Downs escarpment=== [[File:Western_Weald_geology_cross_section.png|thumb|Simplified geological cross section of the western Weald, showing how the land was uplifted to form the [[Weald-Artois anticline]] (dashed lines) and the strata as they are today (solid lines).]] Following the Cretaceous, the sea covering the south of England began to retreat and the land was pushed higher. The Weald (the area covering modern day south Surrey, south Kent and north Sussex) was lifted by [[Alpine orogeny|the same geological processes that created the Alps]], resulting in an [[anticline]] which stretched across the [[English Channel]] to the [[Artois|Artois region]] of northern France. Initially an island, this [[Weald-Artois Anticline|dome-like structure]] was drained by the ancestors of the rivers which today cut through the North and South Downs (including the [[River Mole|Mole]], [[River Wey|Wey]], [[River Arun|Arun]] and [[River Adur|Adur]]). The dome was eroded away over the course of the [[Cenozoic]], exposing the strata beneath and resulting in the escarpments of the Downs and the Greensand Ridge.{{cite book |last1= Gallois |first1= RW |last2= Edmunds |first2= MA |year= 1965 |title= The Wealden District |publisher= British Geological Survey |isbn= 0-11-884078-9}}{{harvnb|Chapman|Young|1979|pp=15–29}} Chalk is a relatively soft rock that may be eroded or weathered in a number of different ways. It is porous, able to absorb up to 20% of its dry weight in water,{{cite journal |vauthors= Burnham CP, Mutter GM |year= 1993 |title= The depth and productivity of chalky soils |journal= Soil Use and Management |volume= 9 |issue= 1 |pages= 1–8 |doi= 10.1111/j.1475-2743.1993.tb00919.x |bibcode= 1993SUMan...9....1B }} and therefore highly susceptible to weathering by [[frost weathering|freeze-thaw action]], which may occur over repeated annual or [[diurnal cycle|diurnal]] cycles. This frost weathering produces a mix of rubble and viscous mud, which may be washed downhill, further eroding the landscape (a process known as [[solifluction]]).{{cite web |url= http://www.mvgs.org.uk/MVGS%20Files/Geomorphology.pdf |title= Geomorphology of the Mole Valley |last= Lester |first= DE |year= 2015 |website= Mole Valley Geological Society |access-date= 17 July 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171116082746/http://www.mvgs.org.uk/MVGS%20Files/Geomorphology.pdf |archive-date= 16 November 2017 |url-status= live }} At the west side of Box Hill, the [[hydraulic action]] of the River Mole has cut a cliff known as The Whites and the river bed contains coarse chalk rubble ([[clastic rock|clast]]), which has fallen from the steep slopes above. Since the chalk contains a very high percentage of [[calcium carbonate]], it can be [[Weathering#Chemical weathering|dissolved by ground water]] and solubilisation of the rock at the base of the hill may have produced the slabwise slumping or subsidence visible at the top of the Burford Spur. Finally, rainwater, which is mildly acidic, will dissolve and react with the chalk.{{cite journal |vauthors= West G, Dumbleton MJ |s2cid= 129120488 |year= 1972 |title= Some observations on swallow holes and mines in the chalk |journal= Quarterly Journal of Engineering Geology |volume= 5 |issue= 1–2 |pages= 171–177 |doi= 10.1144/GSL.QJEG.1972.005.01.16 }} [[File:Headley Heath (geograph 5380860).jpg|thumb|One of two steep-sided combes (dry river valleys) on the western side of Headley Heath.]] The eastern and northern boundaries of Box Hill are defined by [[dry valley|dry river valleys]], now occupied by Pebblehill Road and Headley Lane respectively. These valleys were active during the [[Last Glacial Period|last ice age]], when the chalk bedrock became [[permafrost|frozen]] and [[Permeability (Earth sciences)|impermeable]], forcing water to run over the surface in streams rather than percolating into the ground. Both valleys are narrow, twisting and deep, suggesting that they were created by fast flowing torrents, possibly released during periods of rapid [[snowmelt]].{{refn|Unlike much of Great Britain, Surrey was never covered by permanent [[ice sheets]]. During the [[Last Glacial Maximum]] (corresponding to [[Marine Isotope Stage 5]] - 130,000 to 80,000 years ago), the ice sheets reached as far south as St Albans, approximately {{convert|55|km|mi}} north of Box Hill.{{cite journal |vauthors= Gibbard PL, Clark CD |year= 2011 |title= Pleistocene Glaciation Limits in Great Britain |journal= Developments in Quaternary Science |series= Developments in Quaternary Sciences |volume= 15 |issue= 7 |pages= 75–93 |doi= 10.1016/B978-0-444-53447-7.00007-6|isbn= 9780444534477 }}|group=note}} The northern side of Box Hill (corresponding to the [[dip slope]] of the [[cuesta]] of the North Downs) is cut by six [[combe]]s, also created by Ice Age watercourses. The westernmost of these combes (between the Burford Spur and Lodge Hill) is climbed by the Zig Zag Road. There is a small reservoir to the west of High Ashurst at the base of the Bullen Wood combe, which is not accessible to the public. All six combes contained tributaries of the stream that created the Headley Valley, which joined the [[River Mole]] near Fredley, [[Mickleham, Surrey|Mickleham]].{{harvnb|Hutchings|Bridges|Sankey|1969|p=10}} ===Quarries and lime kilns=== [[File:Betchworth limekiln - geograph.org.uk - 869914.jpg|thumb|right|upright|The Smidth Kiln at [[Betchworth Quarry and Lime Kilns|Betchworth Quarry]] was constructed in around 1901.{{National Heritage List for England|num=1021346}}]] Chalk and flint have been quarried from Box Hill and the surrounding area for many centuries. There are limited surviving examples of the incorporation of chalk blocks (or [[clunch]]) into the stonework of local buildings (including [[Mickleham, Surrey|Mickleham Church]]).{{harvnb|Shepperd|1991|p=112}} Walls made of flints, bound together by [[lime mortar]], are particularly common in [[Surrey]]{{harvnb|Bannister|1999|p=22}} and [[calcium oxide|quicklime]] could be produced with relative ease, by heating chalk above {{convert|825|C|F}} in a [[lime kiln|kiln]].{{cite book |last= Stecher |first= Paul G |year= 1968 |title= The Merck index : an encyclopedia of chemicals and drugs |location= Rahway NJ |publisher= Merck |edition= 8th}} Evidence remains of the small-scale chalk quarrying that occurred prior to the [[Industrial Revolution]], including chalk pits both at Warren Farm and close to the Burford Bridge Hotel. The opening of the [[North Downs Line|Dorking to Reigate railway line]] at the bottom of the hill in 1849, enabled new quarry faces to be opened at [[Brockham]]{{National Heritage List for England|num=1021322}} and [[Betchworth]]. Sidings were provided adjacent to the main line and there was an extensive network of narrow-gauge railway tracks at both sites. The [[Brockham Limeworks]] closed in 1935, however a battery of eight kilns (dating from 1870) still stands and is Grade II listed. The larger [[Betchworth Quarry and Lime Kilns]] (approximately 1 km to the east) closed in 1960 and a variety of different kiln types have been preserved and protected with a Grade II listing. The two sites have been designated as Nature Reserves and are managed by [[Surrey Wildlife Trust]].{{cite web |url= https://www.surreywildlifetrust.org/nature-reserves/betchworth-quarry-lime-kilns |title= Betchworth Quarry & Lime Kilns |author= |publisher= Surrey Wildlife Trust |access-date= 23 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181024192136/https://www.surreywildlifetrust.org/nature-reserves/betchworth-quarry-lime-kilns |archive-date= 24 October 2018 |url-status= live }}{{cite web |url= https://www.surreywildlifetrust.org/nature-reserves/brockham-limeworks |title= Brockham Limeworks |author= |publisher= Surrey Wildlife Trust |access-date= 23 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181024192038/https://www.surreywildlifetrust.org/nature-reserves/brockham-limeworks |archive-date= 24 October 2018 |url-status= live }} A wide range of bat species now roost in the former kilns. Gravel was quarried on the northern side of Headley Heath during the 18th and early 19th centuries, most likely to provide material for building local roads. ===Fossils=== Numerous [[fossil]]s, typical of species living in a warm, shallow sea, have been found in the chalk at Box Hill, including [[brachiopod]]s (''[[Terebratulina gracilis]]'', ''Terebratulina carnea'' and ''Rhynchonella cuvieri''), [[arthropod]]s (''Janira quinquecostatus''), [[bivalvia|bivalves]] (''Spondylus spinosus'' and ''Ostrea hippodium''), [[sea urchin|urchins]] (''Holaster planus'', ''Micraster leskei'') and [[sponge]]s (''Plinthosella squamata'').{{cite journal |vauthors= Young GW |year= 1905 |title= The chalk area of north-east Surrey |journal= Proc. live}} The chalk downland of Box Hill provides a habitat for a wide range of plant species, which in turn support a varied population of insect species. The alkaline soils are thin and nutrient poor, which prevents deeper-rooted lush grasses (with a high water demand) from dominating. Each square metre of chalk downland may support up to 40 different species.{{harvnb|Tuson|2013|p=27}}{{cite web |url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/whats-special-about-chalk-grassland |title= What's special about chalk grassland? |author= |website= National Trust |access-date= 25 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191025110151/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/whats-special-about-chalk-grassland |archive-date= 25 October 2019 |url-status= live }} Without careful management, the grassland would [[ecological succession|revert to woodland]] and so these areas of the hill are [[conservation grazing|grazed]] in order to prevent [[shrubland|scrub]] from becoming overestablished.{{refn|Although its spread is often considered undesirable, scrub provides valuable habitat for a range of invertebrates on Box Hill, including the [[Helix pomatia|Roman snail]], [[rufous grasshopper]] and the [[dark green fritillary]].{{cite web |url= http://www.friendsofboxhill.org.uk/what-we-do-3/conservation/ |title= Box Hill Woodland Plan 2009: The condition and habitat management of the woodland compartments of Box Hill |last1= Dawson |first1= Mark |last2= Creasey |first2= Peter |year= 2009 |website= Friends of Box Hill |location= Dorking |access-date= 27 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191027151825/http://www.friendsofboxhill.org.uk/what-we-do-3/conservation/ |archive-date= 27 October 2019 |url-status= live }}|group=note}} Both the National Trust and Surrey Wildlife Trust use [[Belted Galloway]] cattle (affectionately nicknamed 'Belties'), which crop the grass less hard than other grazers and allow the more delicate wild flowers (including orchids) to flourish. At Betchworth Quarry, Surrey Wildlife Trust allows goats to graze, which can eat woodier plants such as [[Ulex europaeus|gorse]] and [[bramble]]. [[European rabbit|Rabbits]] also make a significant contribution to the control of scrub and coarse grasses on the hill, although their numbers have declined since the introduction of [[myxomatosis]] in 1953.{{harvnb|Chapman|Young|1979|p=95}} [[File:Olympic Rings Box Hill-by-Ian-Capper.jpg|thumb|[[Olympic symbols#Olympic rings|Olympic Rings]] were installed at the viewpoint in July 2012.{{cite news |author= |title= London 2012: Box Hill Olympic road race rings unveiled |url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-surrey-18920560 |work= BBC News |location= London |date= 20 July 2012 |access-date= 25 October 2012 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120829135155/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-surrey-18920560 |archive-date= 29 August 2012 |url-status= live }}]] For any conservation area, it is important to find a balance between the interests of people visiting and the needs of the wildlife that it seeks to protect. international importance. Common [[Canopy (biology)|canopy-layer]] species include [[Fagus sylvatica|beech]], [[Fraxinus excelsior|ash]] and [[Quercus robur|oak]]. [[Understory|Understorey]] species include [[Ilex aquifolium|holly]], [[Corylus avellana|hazel]], [[Sambucus|elder]] and [[honeysuckle]]. [[Invasive species]] found on the hill include [[Buddleja|buddleia]], [[Prunus laurocerasus|cherry laurel]], [[Reynoutria japonica|Japanese knot weed]] and [[Solidago canadensis|Canadian goldenrod]]. [[Boxwood blight]], a [[pathogenic fungus|fungal disease]] caused by [[Cylindrocladium|''Cylindrocladium buxicola'']], is widespread. ====Bats==== Several abandoned brick and concrete structures provide habitats for [[bat]]s and grills have been placed over their entrances to protect the roosting sites. Three species are known to inhabit the old Box Hill Fort: the [[brown long-eared bat]], the [[common noctule|noctule bat]] and [[Natterer's bat]].{{harvnb|Tuson|2013|p=22}} The brown long-eared bat, Natterer's bat, the [[whiskered bat]] and [[Daubenton's bat]] have been recorded at both Betchworth and Brockham quarries. [[Brandt's bat]] has been recorded at Betchworth; [[Bechstein's bat]] and the [[common pipistrelle]] have been recorded at Brockham. ====Butterflies and moths==== {{multiple image | width = 110 | footer = [[Chalkhill blue]] (left) and [[Melanargia galathea|marbled white]] (right) butterflies on [[Centaurea nigra|knapweed]] flowers on Box Hill. | image1 = Lysandra coridon on Box Hill.jpg | alt1 = | caption1 = | image2 = Melanargia galathea on Box Hill-by-Ian-Capper.jpg | alt2 = | caption2 = }} Box Hill supports 38 different species of butterflies. Species include [[Hesperia comma|silver-spotted skipper]], [[Adonis blue]] and [[Lysandra coridon|chalkhill blue]] (grassland); [[brown hairstreak]] (scrub); [[Apatura iris|purple emperor]] and [[Limenitis camilla|white admiral]] (woodland).{{cite web |url= https://butterfly-conservation.org/in-your-area/surrey-and-sw-london-branch/sites-species |title= Sites & Species |author= |website= Butterfly Conservation |access-date= 5 July 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200706140214/https://butterfly-conservation.org/in-your-area/surrey-and-sw-london-branch/sites-species |archive-date= 6 July 2020 |url-status= live }} The [[small pearl-bordered fritillary]] was present on the hill in the 1970s,{{harvnb|Chapman|Young|1979|p=97}} but has not been recorded locally since 1997. [[Anthyllis vulneraria|Kidney vetch]], growing in the Zig Zag Valley and below the Viewpoint, supports populations of the [[small blue]].{{cite web |url= http://www.molevalley.gov.uk/CausewayDocList/DocServlet?ref=MO/2012/0536&docid=404511 |title= Box Hill Ecological Report, November, 2011 |website= Mole Valley District Council |access-date= 25 October 2019 |archive-date= 2 January 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210102103210/https://www.molevalley.gov.uk/CausewayDocList/DocServlet?ref=MO%2F2012%2F0536&docid=404511 |url-status= live }}{{cite web |url= https://butterfly-conservation.org/sites/default/files/1-skipper-2017-10.pdf |title= Small Blue update |last= Jeffcoate |first= Gail |year= 2017 |website= Surrey Skipper |publisher= Butterfly Conservation |access-date= 25 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200128164700/https://butterfly-conservation.org/sites/default/files/1-skipper-2017-10.pdf |archive-date= 28 January 2020 |url-status= live }} To create new habitats for the butterflies, a number of ‘scrapes’ were excavated in the late 2010s, exposing bare chalk on which vetch can become established with minimal competition. Buddleia removal was also initiated as part of the same programme.{{cite web |url= https://butterfly-conservation.org/sites/default/files/2019-10/Surrey%20Small%20Blue%20Stepping%20Stones%20Report%202019-10b.pdf |title= Report: Surrey Small Blue Stepping Stones Project 2017 to 2019 |last= Haynes |first= Fiona |year= 2019 |publisher= Butterfly Conservation |access-date= 5 July 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200128164825/https://butterfly-conservation.org/sites/default/files/2019-10/Surrey%20Small%20Blue%20Stepping%20Stones%20Report%202019-10b.pdf |archive-date= 28 January 2020 |url-status= live }} Rare moth species found on the hill include the [[Aspitates gilvaria|straw belle]], [[Scotopteryx bipunctaria|chalk carpet]], [[Scopula ornata|lace border]], [[Synanthedon andrenaeformis|orange-tailed clearwing]] and the [[Phyllonorycter scabiosella|Surrey midget moth]]. ====Other insects==== The hill has given its name to a species of [[Coreidae|squash bug]], now found throughout south-east England. ==Recreation== [[File:Box_Hill_Salomons_Memorial.jpg|thumb|Salomons Memorial viewpoint, looking south, in 2010]] ===Box Hill Country Park=== The western part of Box Hill, managed by the [[National Trust]], was designated a [[Country Park]] in 1971{{harvnb|Littledale|Locock|Sankey|1984|p=5}} and some of the outbuildings associated with the Box Hill Fort are in use as a visitor centre, gift shop and servery. In 2011, a ''Natural Play Trail'' was constructed close to the visitor centre, cofunded by the National Trust and the Friends of Box Hill.{{cite web |url= https://www.surreylife.co.uk/out-about/walks/national-trust-s-new-natural-play-trail-at-box-hill-1-1644611 |title= National Trust's new natural play trail at Box Hill |last= Brien |first= Emma |date= 24 November 2011 |website= Surrey Life |access-date= 29 February 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200229122938/https://www.surreylife.co.uk/out-about/walks/national-trust-s-new-natural-play-trail-at-box-hill-1-1644611 |archive-date= 29 February 2020 |url-status= live }} On the hill there are [[Parking lot|car parks]]{{cite news |author= |title= Box Hill, Surrey: walk of the week |url= https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/activityandadventure/walkingholidays/8356605/Box-Hill-Surrey-walk-of-the-week.html |date= 2 March 2011 |access-date= 19 October 2019 |work= Daily Telegraph |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110309211404/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/activityandadventure/walkingholidays/8356605/Box-Hill-Surrey-walk-of-the-week.html |archive-date= 9 March 2011 |url-status= live }} and a panoramic view over the [[Weald]] towards the [[South Downs]] may be enjoyed from the Salomons Memorial (more commonly known as the viewpoint).{{refn|A common misconception is that the Salomons Memorial (at {{convert|172|m|ft|abbr=on}} [[Ordnance Datum|above OD]]) marks the highest point of the hill, however the land continues to rise to the east. The true summit of the hill is at Betchworth Clump at {{convert|224|m|ft|abbr=on}} above OD and is currently occupied by a water tower and transmitter mast. |group=note}} Juniper Top, on the northern side of the hill, offers views to the northwest towards [[Windsor Castle]].
