undergone several alterations from the 2012 Olympic course, the two races always include a climb of Box Hill. ===High Ashurst=== {{Main|High Ashurst}} High Ashurst is an [[outdoor education]] and [[outdoor recreation|activity]] centre on the northern side of Box Hill, adjacent to Headley Heath. The centre is run by Surrey Outdoor Learning and Development on behalf of [[Surrey County Council]].{{cite web |url= https://www.surreyoutdoorlearning.uk |title= Surrey Outdoor Learning and Development |author= |access-date= 16 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191016222640/https://www.surreyoutdoorlearning.uk/ |archive-date= 16 October 2019 |url-status= live }} Previously the site comprised the grounds of a country house, which was demolished in the 1970s, having been derelict for several decades. ===Boidier Hurst campsite=== The District [[The Scout Association|Scout Associations]] of [[Leatherhead]] and [[Epsom and Ewell]] own a {{convert|10|acre|ha|adj=on|order=flip}} [[campsite]], located between Box Hill village and Headley Heath.{{cite web |url= http://www.boidierhurst.org.uk/index.html |title= Boidier Hurst Scout campsite |author= |website= Boidier Hurst Scout campsite |access-date= 1 March 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200301083815/http://www.boidierhurst.org.uk/index.html |archive-date= 1 March 2020 |url-status= live }}{{cite web |url= http://www.boidierhurst.org.uk/the-site.html |title= The site |author= |website= Boidier Hurst Scout campsite |access-date= 1 March 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200301083814/http://www.boidierhurst.org.uk/the-site.html |archive-date= 1 March 2020 |url-status= live }} There are 11 areas for pitching groups of tents, set within [[coppicing|coppiced]] [[Aesculus hippocastanum|chestnut]] woodland. Washing, toilet facilities and a kitchen are available.{{cite web |url= http://www.boidierhurst.org.uk/manly-building.html |title= The Manly Building |author= |website= Boidier Hurst Scout campsite |access-date= 1 March 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200301083815/http://www.boidierhurst.org.uk/manly-building.html |archive-date= 1 March 2020 |url-status= live }} Use of Boidier Hurst is restricted to members of The Scout Association, [[Girlguiding|The Guide Association]] and to local school groups on [[The Duke of Edinburgh's Award|Duke of Edinburgh's Award]] expeditions. ==Points of interest== ===Betchworth Clump=== The highest point on Box Hill is immediately to the east of Box Hill village at {{convert|224|m|ft|abbr=on}} [[Ordnance Datum|above OD]]. The area is known as Betchworth Clump after a distinctive group of beech trees, which were present at the start of the 20th century.{{cite book |last= Malden |first= Henry Elliot |year= 1902–1914 |title= The Victoria history of the county of Surrey |location= Westminster |publisher= Archibald Constable |page= 166 }} Today, the dense woodland at the summit conceals a [[water tower]] and [[Radio masts and towers|transmitter mast]], neither of which are accessible to the public. The concrete water tower was built in 1930 by East Surrey Water, the forerunner of [[SES Water]]. The structure was refurbished in 2009 to extend its working life by at least 25 years; modifications included the relining of the water bowl, repair of cracks in the walls and roof, as well as the provision of a new access staircase.{{cite web |url= https://www.edie.net/library/CRL-gets-started-on-water-tower-repairs/5046 |title= CRL gets started on water tower repairs |author= |date= 10 June 2009 |website= edie.net |access-date= 1 March 2020 |archive-date= 2 January 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210102103226/https://www.edie.net/library/CRL-gets-started-on-water-tower-repairs/5046 |url-status= live }} The 30m-high mobile phone mast was constructed in 2003 and is operated by [[Vodafone]] and [[EE Limited]]. ===Broadwood's Folly=== [[File:Broadwood's_Tower-cropped.jpg|thumb|Broadwood's Folly was built in around 1820.{{National Heritage List for England|num=1391454}} Part of the Zig Zag Road is visible to the right of the tower.]] The circular flint tower located on the northern tip of Lodge Hill was built for the piano maker [[Broadwood and Sons|Thomas Broadwood]], who purchased [[Juniper Hall]] in 1815.{{harvnb|Wainwright|1982|p=338}}{{cite web |url= http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-494323-the-broadwood-folly-at-juniper-hall-dork |title= The Broadwood Folly at Juniper Hall, Mickleham |author= Goodge M |year= 2005 |publisher= British Listed Buildings |access-date= 28 April 2011 |archive-date= 2 January 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210102103313/https://britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101391454-the-broadwood-folly-at-juniper-hall-mickleham |url-status= live }} It is approximately {{convert|8|m|ft}} high and originally had two internal floors, linked by a spiral staircase. The original doorway is visible on the east side, but has been sealed with rough flints. An avenue of beech trees linked the folly to Juniper Hall, although these were destroyed by the [[Great Storm of 1987]]. The tower may have been built to commemorate the [[Battle of Waterloo]].{{harvnb|Headley|Meulenkamp|1986|p=118}} A [[sparkling wine]], produced by [[Denbies Wine Estate]] for the [[Lidl]] supermarket chain, has been named after the folly.{{cite news |last= Williams |first= David |date= 18 September 2016 |title= National treasures: Welcome to the new world of English and Welsh wines |url= https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2016/sep/18/six-of-the-best-english-wines |work= The Guardian |location= London |access-date= 26 October 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191026113708/https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2016/sep/18/six-of-the-best-english-wines |archive-date= 26 October 2019 |url-status= live }} ===Labilliere's grave=== [[File:Peter Labelliere's grave, Box Hill.JPG|upright|thumb|Labilliere's tombstone]] [[Peter Labilliere]] was born in [[Dublin]] on 30 May 1725 to a family of French [[Huguenot]] descent. He joined the British Army at the age of 14, becoming a major in 1760.{{harvnb|Lander|2000|pp=7–8}} After leaving the army he became a political agitator and was accused in 1775 of bribing British troops not to fight in the American War of Independence, although he was never tried for treason.{{harvnb|Lander|2000|pp=20–21}} After moving to Dorking in around 1789, Labilliere often visited Box Hill to meditate.{{harvnb|Lander|2000|pp=35–36}} With old age he became increasingly eccentric and neglected his own personal hygiene to such an extent that he acquired the nickname "the walking dung-hill". He died on 6 June 1800.{{harvnb|Timbs|1877}} In accordance with his wishes he was [[Burial#Inverted burial|buried head downwards]], on 11 June on the western side of Box Hill above The Whites. In the presence of a crowd of thousands that included visitors from London as well as the local "quality gentry",[https://www.getsurrey.co.uk/news/nostalgia/major-peter-labelliere-strange-history-13643026 Major Peter Labelliere: Strange history of man buried upside down atop Box Hill] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226091910/https://www.getsurrey.co.uk/news/nostalgia/major-peter-labelliere-strange-history-13643026 |date=26 February 2018 }}, Surrey Mirror, by W. H. Chouler, July 1963 Labilliere was buried without any religious ceremony, having reportedly said that the world was "topsy-turvey" and that it would be righted in the end if he were interred thus. However, in his "Book of Devotions", he wrote that he wished to emulate the example of [[Saint Peter|St Peter]], who was [[Cross of St. Peter|crucified upside-down]] according to tradition.{{harvnb|Lander|2000|pp=39–40}}{{cite journal |last= Gittings |first= Clare |s2cid= 143937885 |date= 20 November 2017 |title= Eccentric or enlightened? Unusual burial and commemoration in England, 1689 - 1823 |journal= Mortality |volume= 12 |issue= 4 |pages= 321–349 |doi= 10.1080/13576270701609667}} The current memorial stone on Box Hill is not believed to mark the exact location of his burial (which is thought to be several metres to the west on a steep incline). There are two errors on the stone itself: He was buried in ''June'' 1800 (rather than July) and all surviving manuscripts indicate that he spelt his name Lab'''i'''lliere (rather than Lab'''e'''lliere).{{harvnb|Lander|2000|p=6}}{{cite web |last=No |first=Doilum |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/doilum/387839851/ |title=Box Hill, Surrey sur Flickr : partage de photos ! |publisher=Flickr.com |access-date=27 July 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120916082840/http://www.flickr.com/photos/doilum/387839851 |archive-date=16 September 2012 |url-status=live }} ===Weypole and Stepping Stones=== [[File:Stepping stones.jpg|right|thumb|The Stepping Stones at the foot of Box Hill. The photograph is taken from the west bank of the Mole, looking across the river to the Weypole.]] The Weypole (or Waypole) is a roughly semi-circular {{convert|2.4|ha|acre|abbr=on|adj=on}} area of level ground at the foot of Box Hill, between The Whites and the River Mole. It was originally part of the grounds of Burford Lodge, built by John Eckersall in 1776, and the prevalence of apple and cherry trees suggests that it was used as an orchard for a time.{{harvnb|Chapman|Young|1979|p=164}} The Burford Lodge estate was later owned by the horticulturalist [[Sir Trevor Lawrence, 2nd Baronet|Sir Trevor Lawrence]], who created a garden along the banks of the Mole for his collection of orchids.{{harvnb|Chadwick|Chadwick|2006|p=121}} A ford across the River Mole is thought to have existed here since prehistoric times.{{harvnb|Ashton|Blight|2006|p=65}} The ''way-pole'' was a [[notch (engineering)|notched]] post, secured in the riverbed to indicate the depth of the water.{{cite journal |author=A Son of the Marshed |year=1890 |title=A Surrey River |journal= The Living Age |volume= 185 |issue=2395 |pages=486–497 |publisher=Littell}} Stepping stones at this site are first recorded in 1841 and they may have been installed by an owner of Burford Lodge to facilitate access to the Weypole orchard.{{harvnb|Brayley|Britton|1841|p=179}} The crossing was formally reopened on 11 September 1946 by Prime Minister [[Clement Attlee]], at the request of [[James Chuter Ede]], a local politician and Attlee's Home Secretary.Chuter Ede papers collection, Surrey History Centre, 6408/13 The new stones replaced those removed during the Second World War as an anti-invasion measure.{{cite magazine |year= 1946 |title= Picture of the Week |magazine= Life |volume= 21 |issue= 13 |page= 36 |publisher= Time Inc.}}{{refn|Chuter Ede paid for the reinstatement of the stones, a total of £156 19s 6d. He commented that the cost of the work was "considerably higher than I expected".{{harvnb|Hart|2021|pp=180–181}}|group=note}} The location is popular with both anglers and families, although swimming is strongly discouraged. The stones give their name to the pub in the nearby village of [[Westhumble]]. ===Other=== The [[Burford Bridge Hotel]] and [[Juniper Hall]] Field Studies Centre lie at the foot of Box Hill close to the river Mole. Both are rich in historical associations with famous visitors and residents. ==Notable former residents== ===John Logie Baird=== [[John Logie Baird]] (1888-1946), the inventor of the [[history of television|first working television system]], lived at Box Hill from 1929 until 1932.{{harvnb|Burns|2000|page=205}} He had first demonstrated the new technology in early 1926,{{cite journal |vauthors= McLean DF |s2cid= 110636009 |year= 2014 |title= The Achievement of Television: The Quality and Features of John Logie Baird's System in 1926 |journal= International Journal for the History of Engineering & Technology |volume= 84 |issue= 2 |pages= 227–247 |doi=10.1179/1758120614Z.00000000048 }} and continued with his work when he moved to Swiss Cottage on the top of the hill. He installed a small-scale electricity generating plant in a purpose-built outbuilding, to provide electrical power for his experiments, which included test transmissions to the roof of the Red Lion [[pub]] in [[Dorking]] High Street.{{National Heritage List for England|num=1393745}} He also demonstrated his Noctovisor, an [[infrared]] viewing device, which was designed to enable ships to see each other at night or in fog.{{cite web|url=http://geocities.com/neveyaakov/electro_science/baird.html |title=Baird |date=27 October 2009 |access-date=27 July 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091027123028/http://geocities.com/neveyaakov/electro_science/baird.html |archive-date=27 October 2009 }} Swiss Cottage was built in the mid-19th century and is protected by a Grade II listing. It is not accessible to the public. ===Brodie family=== Brockham Warren was the family seat of the [[Brodie baronets]].{{cite web|url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/surrey/vol3/pp166-173 |title=Parishes: Betchworth |work=A History of the County of Surrey |publisher=[[Victoria County History]] |page=167}}{{cite web |url= http://www.brockhamhistory.org/brockham-people/sir-benjamin-collins-brodie/ |title= Sir Benjamin Collins Brodie |last= Hines |first= T |website= Brockham History |access-date= 29 July 2020 |archive-date= 2 January 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210102103125/http://www.brockhamhistory.org/brockham-people/sir-benjamin-collins-brodie/ |url-status= live }} [[Sir Benjamin Collins Brodie, 1st Baronet]] (1783-1862) was a [[physiologist]] and [[surgery|surgeon]], who performed pioneering research into bone and joint diseases. He served as sergeant-surgeon to both [[William IV of the United Kingdom|William IV]] and subsequently [[Victoria of the United Kingdom|Queen Victoria]]. He was made a [[baronet]] in 1834 and was President of the [[Royal Society]] from 1858 to 1861.{{EB1911|inline=1|wstitle=Brodie, Sir Benjamin Collins|volume=4|page=625}} His son, [[Sir Benjamin Collins Brodie, 2nd Baronet]] (1817-1880), was a Chemistry Professor at [[Oxford University]] from 1865 to 1872, and is chiefly known for his investigations into the [[allotropes of carbon|allotropic states of carbon]] and for his discovery of [[graphite oxide|graphitic acid]].{{cite journal | last1 = Brodie | first1 = B. C. | doi = 10.1098/rstl.1859.0013 | title = On the Atomic Weight of Graphite | journal = Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London | volume = 149 | pages = 249–259 | year = 1859 | url = https://archive.org/details/philtrans03630074 | jstor = 108699 | bibcode=1859RSPT..149..249B| doi-access = free }} ===George Meredith=== [[File:George_Meredith's_Home.jpg|thumb|George Meredith and family members, photographed in the rear garden of Flint Cottage, Box Hill.]] The author [[George Meredith]] (1828-1909) lived in Flint Cottage from 1868 until his death. He built a chalet in the garden in which he wrote. Today the house is protected by a Grade II listing and is not accessible to the public.{{National Heritage List for England|num=1278478}} Among several works written at Box Hill, Meredith's poem ''[[The Lark Ascending]]'', published in 1881, inspired [[Ralph Vaughan Williams]] to compose the [[The Lark Ascending (Vaughan Williams)|musical work of the same name]].{{cite web |url= https://www.bl.uk/collection-items/vaughan-williams-the-lark-ascending |title= Ralph Vaughan Williams: The Lark Ascending |author= |publisher= British Library |access-date= 19 July 2020 |archive-date= 2 January 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210102103127/https://www.bl.uk/collection-items/vaughan-williams-the-lark-ascending |url-status= live }} A second poem, ''[[s:Poems and Lyrics of the Joy of Earth/Love in the Valley|Love in the Valley]]'' (published in 1883 as part of a collection entitled ''Poems and Lyrics of the Joy of Earth''), is said to have been inspired by the part of Box Hill known as Juniper Bottom or Happy Valley.{{cite journal |last= Pevy |first= M |year= 2003 |title= Box Hill |journal= Surrey Archaeological Society Bulletin |volume= 368 |pages= 13–14 |url= https://www.surreyarchaeology.org.uk/sites/default/files/SAS368_0.pdf |access-date= 26 September 2020 |archive-date= 2 January 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210102103055/https://www.surreyarchaeology.org.uk/sites/default/files/SAS368_0.pdf |url-status= live }} The part of the hill immediately opposite the cottage is known as ''Barrie's Bank'', because the author [[J. M. Barrie]] supposedly waited there, while summoning the courage to introduce himself to Meredith.{{harvnb|Tuson|2013|p=18}} ===E. F. Warburg=== The botanist [[E. F. Warburg|Edmund Frederic ("Heff") Warburg]] (1908-1966) grew up at Boidier, a house close to the southeastern corner of Headley Heath. Heff became [[Reader (academic rank)|reader]] in [[plant taxonomy]] at [[Oxford University]] and was a [[fellow]] of [[New College, Oxford|New College]].{{cite journal |vauthors= Smith AJ |year= 1967 |title= Obituary: Dr E F Warburg |url= http://archive.bsbi.org.uk/Proc7p67.pdf |journal= Proc. [[Surrey Wildlife Trust]] manage [[Brockham Limeworks]] (owned by [[Surrey County Council]]) as well as [[Betchworth Quarry and Lime Kilns]] (privately owned). Both Trusts rely on the support of volunteer groups, working alongside paid employees, to carry out conservation and education work. The ''Friends of Box Hill'' (FoBH) is a local organisation, which supports the National Trust in its work in the Country Park. Several of its members advise the Trust on its wildlife management plans and the FoBH also fund specific projects, including the purchase of equipment and improvement of visitor facilities. They also organise a programme of social events, which includes regular talks by Trust staff.{{cite web |url= http://www.friendsofboxhill.org.uk/what-we-do-3/ |title= What we do |website= Friends of Box Hill |access-date= 29 February 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191027151842/http://www.friendsofboxhill.org.uk/what-we-do-3/ |archive-date= 27 October 2019 |url-status= live }} The ''Friends of Headley Heath'' (FoHH) coordinate volunteer working parties to assist National Trust Rangers and also run a series of social events.{{cite web |url= http://www.headleysurrey.org.uk/fohh.htm |title= Friends of Headley Heath |website= Headley Village Website |access-date= 29 February 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191021191617/http://www.headleysurrey.org.uk/fohh.htm |archive-date= 21 October 2019 |url-status= live }} (Both the FoBH and FoHH are independent of the National Trust.) ==Transport links== ===Public transport=== {{stnlink|Box Hill & Westhumble}} is the closest railway station to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] Country Park (approximately 500 m) and is served by trains from both [[London Victoria station|London Victoria]] and [[London Waterloo station|London Waterloo]]. Coats, ''Garden Shrubs and Their Histories'' (1964) 1992, ''s.v.'' "Buxus". [[Daniel Defoe]] (the author of ''[[Robinson Crusoe]]'') was educated for five years (until around the age of fourteen) at the Rev. James Fisher's boarding school in Pixham Lane, Dorking. He writes extensively about the area around Box Hill in his travelogue, ''[[A tour thro' the whole island of Great Britain]]'' (1724–1727), which describes the country shortly before the start of the [[Industrial Revolution]].{{cite journal |author= Bastian F |year= 1957 |title= Daniel Defoe and the Dorking District |journal= Surrey Archaeological Collections |volume= 55 |pages= 41–64 |url= https://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/catalogue/adsdata/arch-379-1/dissemination/pdf/vol_55/surreyac055_041-064_bastian.pdf |access-date= 27 September 2020 |doi= 10.5284/1068897 |archive-date= 2 January 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210102102002/https://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archiveDS/archiveDownload?t=arch-379-1%2Fdissemination%2Fpdf%2Fvol_55%2Fsurreyac055_041-064_bastian.pdf |url-status= live }} He records that in the late 17th century, [[Sir Adam Browne, 2nd Baronet|Sir Adam Browne]] the then landowner, approved the fitting out of a cave or vault close to what is now the Salomons Memorial, to supply 'refreshment' to visitors to the hill. A group of young [[English Dissenters|Dissenters]] from [[Dorking]] were so disgusted by the 'debauched' behaviour that the sale of alcohol encouraged (which took place even on Sundays), that they stormed up the hill one Saturday night and blew up the cavern with gunpowder. The writer Edward Beavan describes the hill and the surrounding area of Surrey in his poem ''Box-Hill, a descriptive poem'', published in 1777.{{sfn|Beavan|1777}} [[File: Hammond-Emma22 (recadrée).jpg|thumb|upright|The Picnic at Box Hill: Pen-and-ink drawing by Chris Hammond (1860–1900) for the 1898 edition of ''[[Emma (novel)|Emma]]'' by [[Jane Austen]].]] The '[[s:Emma/Volume 3/Chapter 7|picnic scene]]', a pivotal passage of [[Jane Austen]]'s novel ''[[Emma (novel)|Emma]]'' (first published in 1815) is set at Box Hill.{{cite book |last1=Austen |first1=Jane |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/158/158-h/158-h.htm |title=Emma |access-date=2 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180903013329/https://www.gutenberg.org/files/158/158-h/158-h.htm |archive-date=3 September 2018 |url-status=live |via=Project Gutenberg}} [[Celia Fiennes]], a contemporary of Defoe, described Box Hill in her travel memoirs, which were published in 1888 (almost 150 years after her death) under the title ''Through England on a Side Saddle''.{{harvnb|Fiennes|1888|pp=289–290}}{{cite journal |vauthors= Taylor EG |year= 1948 |title= England of the Glorious Revolution |journal= The Geographical Journal |volume= 111 |issue= 1 |pages= 101–104 |doi= 10.2307/1789289 |jstor= 1789289 }} :"Box Hill… is the Continuation of the Ridge of hills I mentiond by Maidstone; its a Greate height and shows you a vast precipice down on the farther side, and such a vast vale full of woods Enclosures and Little towns. There is a very good river that runs by a Little town Called Darken just at the foote of this hill, very famous for good troutts and great store of ffish. On this hill the top is Cover'd with box whence its name proceeds, and there is other wood but its all Cutt in Long private walks very shady and pleasant, and this is a great diversion to the Company and would be more ffrequented if nearer Epsom town." In ''England: A Nation'', (London: R. Brimley Johnson, 1904), edited by Lucian Oldershaw, and in a chapter entitled "The Patriotic Idea" written by [[G. K. Chesterton]], the beauty of Box Hill violated by an invading army is used to express a healthy patriot's love for his nation as opposed to the jingoistic nationalism of tabloid newspapers:{{cite book |last= Chesterton |first=GK |author-link= G. K. Chesterton |editor-last= Oldershaw |editor-first= Lucian |title=England: A Nation |publisher= R. Brimley Johnson |location= London |date=1904 |pages=100–110 |chapter=Chapter 1: The Patriotic Idea |url= https://archive.org/stream/englandnationbei00patrrich/englandnationbei00patrrich_djvu.txt}} :"But just as a man who has been in love will find it difficult to write a whole frantic epic about a flirtation, so all that kind of rhetoric about the Union Jack and the Anglo-Saxon blood, which has made amusing the journalism of this country for the last six years, will be merely impossible to the man who has for one moment called up before himself what would be the real sensation of hearing that a foreign army was encamped on Box Hill." '''Abinger Hammer''' is a village in the [[Mole Valley]] district of [[Surrey]], England. It lies in the [[Vale of Holmesdale]] in the [[Surrey Hills National Landscape]] and is located on the [[A25 road|A25]] about {{convert|6|mi}} east of [[Guildford]] and {{convert|4+1/2|mi}} west of [[Dorking]]. The village is named after its water-powered iron [[forge]].

== Geography ==
Abinger Hammer lies within the parish of [[Abinger]] which includes [[Abinger Common]] and [[Sutton Abinger]]. Other neighbouring villages are [[Wotton, Surrey|Wotton]] and [[Gomshall]].

The [[River Tillingbourne]] flows through the village.

== History ==
[[Image:abingersign.jpg|150px|thumb|left|Abinger Hammer was a focus for [[forge]]s]]
[[File:Abinger hammer clock.jpg|thumb|upright|Abinger Hammer clock]]
The river Tillingbourne was enchannelled in the 16th century, creating a hammer pond, provided water power for Abinger Hammer Mill which worked [[Sussex iron industry|Sussex-sourced iron]].<ref>Pearce, H, ''Hammer and Furnace Ponds'', Pomegranate Press, 2011</ref> The pond has since been adapted for the cultivation of watercress.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hammerpond.org.uk/Gazetteer/Surrey/surrey.htm|title = SURREY}}</ref><ref name="AHM">[http://www.tillingbournetales.co.uk/places/mills/abinger-hammer-mill/ ''Abinger Hammer Mill''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180307023526/http://www.tillingbournetales.co.uk/places/mills/abinger-hammer-mill/ |date=7 March 2018 }} at www.tillingbournetales.co.uk. Retrieved 30 Apr 2017.</ref>

Abinger hammer mill was in operation during the second half of the 16th century. The reputed manufacture of guns for use against the [[Spanish Armada]] has no basis in fact; the mill being incapable of casting iron. The waters of the Tillingbourne powered the water wheel which drove the heavy {{cvt|400|kg}}, hammer of the forge. The forge closed in 1787 despite attempts to save or convert it.<ref name="AHM"/> A contemporary forge, [[Finch Foundry]], survives in Devon.
 
The clock which overhangs the main road portrays the figure of "Jack the Blacksmith", who strikes the hour with his hammer. The clock bears the motto "By me you know how fast to go". The clock was given in memory of the first [[Thomas Farrer, 1st Baron Farrer|Lord Farrer of Abinger Hall]] who died in 1899. The clock represents the iron industry and the role played by the county of Surrey in the industrial past.<ref>[http://www.ukattraction.com/south-east-england/abinger-hammer-village-clock.htm UK attractions] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061231022529/http://www.ukattraction.com/south-east-england/abinger-hammer-village-clock.htm |date=December 31, 2006 }} retrieved 6-1-07</ref>

==Transport==
The A25 runs through the village. Abinger is approximately {{convert|1|mi}} east of [[Gomshall railway station]] on the [[North Downs Line]] between [[Redhill, Surrey|Redhill]] and Guildford.

== Sights ==
[[Image:Womensbikerace2012.JPG|thumb|upright|The 2012 Women's Olympic Cycle Race passing through Abinger Hammer on its way to Box Hill]]
In summer the village green in Abinger is popular with locals and tourists who like to picnic on the grass whilst watching a game of [[cricket]] in surroundings which are quintessentially English. The cricket pitch borders the Tillingbourne – the Post Office sells nets for children to "fish" in this shallow and sandy stream. Annie's tearoom is next to the Post Office and offers lunches and teas seven days a week.

== Education ==
After Abinger Hammer village school was closed by the LEA in 1982, the local community took over the running of it. As of 2008 the school had only sixteen students. A small group of trustees worked to raise funds to maintain the building and to pay the staff but the number of students reduced further, until the school was forced to close in July 2009.<ref>[https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/125430 Department for Education website] retrieved 30-8-21</ref>

== Nature ==
[[Oxmoor Copse]] is an [[AONB|Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]], recognised for its plant species and its aesthetic quality. It is south of the village.

== People ==
During the years 1925 to 1945, the novelist [[E. M. Forster]] lived in Abinger Hammer with his mother Alice Clare, in a house designed by his father, the architect Eddie Morgan Forster. The house had previously been occupied by his aunt Laura.<ref>[https://www.heureka.clara.net/surrey-hants/surrey-writers.htm] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304024259/https://www.heureka.clara.net/surrey-hants/surrey-writers.htm |date=March 4, 2016 }}</ref> Forster was obliged to leave this home in 1946 as the landlord refused to renew the lease.<ref>Furbank, P. N. ''E. M. Forster, A Life.'' vol 2. London: Secker and Warburg, 1978.</ref>

[[Edward Wilkins Waite]] (1854–1924), landscape painter, lived for a time at Abinger Hammer. He was born in [[Leatherhead]], Surrey, and much of his work depicted rural scenes in the county – including at least one picture, [[:File:Edward Wilkins Waite03.jpg|''Old Willows'']], painted in the vicinity of the village.

[[David Nobbs]] gave Abinger Hammer as the location of the home of Uncle Percy Spillinger, played by late actor [[Tony Sympson]], in Episode 4, Series 1 of ''[[The Fall and Rise of Reginald Perrin]]''.

The actor [[John Gordon Sinclair]] lives in Abinger Hammer.

== Abinger Hall ==
Abinger Hammer is also home to Abinger Hall, a late 18th-century country estate, which has since fallen into disrepair.<ref name="parks">{{cite web |title=Abinger Hall |url=https://www.parksandgardens.org/places/abinger-hall |website=www.parksandgardens.org }}</ref> Abinger Hall was the home of [[William Scarlett, 3rd Baron Abinger|William Frederick Scarlett]], Baron Abinger and Helen Scarlett, Lady Abinger. It was also the birthplace of [[Ella Campbell Scarlett]], who was the first female doctor of the state of [[Bloemfontein]], South Africa.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Potgieter |first1=S V |title=History of Medicine: Medicine in Bloemfontein – anecdotes from the turn of the century |journal=South African Medical Journal |date=1998 |volume=3 |issue=88 |pages=272–274 |url=https://www.ajol.info/index.php/samj/article/viewFile/148964/138466}}</ref> The Victorian house was demolished in 1959.<ref name="parks "/>

1029643.title: Clandon Park House
1029643.extract:
Clandon Park House is an early 18th-century grade I listed Palladian mansion in West Clandon, near Guildford in Surrey.
It stands in the south east corner of Clandon Park, a 220-hectare (540-acre) agricultural parkland estate which has been the seat of the Earls of Onslow for over two centuries. The house and gardens were given to the National Trust in 1956, but the park remains in private ownership. Some of the house's contents have also been acquired by the Trust in lieu of estate duty.
Construction of the house, designed by Italian architect Giacomo Leoni, began about 1730, and the interiors were finished by continental sculptors and plasterers in the 1740s. It replaced an Elizabethan house. The park was landscaped by Lancelot 'Capability' Brown in 1781, and there are two formal gardens on either side of the house. On the Epsom Road, leading to the park and house, are the Grade II* 18th century wrought iron gates with armorial overthrow, which Brown installed, and the gatehouses (1776), designed by Brown himself.
Near the house is a Māori meeting house, one of only four outside New Zealand, that was brought to England in the late 19th century. After being transferred to the National Trust, the house underwent restoration before it was opened to the public, and later became a wedding venue and filming location for period dramas.
Clandon Park House was badly damaged by fire in April 2015, probably caused by an electrical fault in the basement, leaving it "essentially a shell". Only one room, the Speaker's Parlour, was left intact. Thousands of historic artefacts, paintings, and items of furniture were lost in what has been described as a national tragedy. In January 2016, the National Trust announced that some of the principal rooms on the ground floor would be fully restored to the original 18th-century designs, and upper floors will be used for exhibitions and events. However, the Trust announced in 2022 its intention to restore only the Speaker's Parlour, the exterior walls, the roof and the windows and conserve the rest of the house in its ruined state while making it accessible to the public. Building work is due to start in autumn 2025 and the property expected to reopen in 2029.

'''Clandon Park House''' is an early 18th-century [[Listed building|grade I listed]] [[Palladian]] mansion in [[West Clandon]], near [[Guildford]] in Surrey.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1294591|desc=Clandon Park|accessdate=7 November 2014}}</ref>

It stands in the south east corner of '''Clandon Park''', a {{convert|220|ha|acre|adj=on}} agricultural parkland estate which has been the seat of the [[Earls of Onslow]] for over two centuries. The house and gardens were given to the [[National Trust]] in 1956,<ref name="Airs2002">{{cite book|author=Malcolm Airs|title=The Twentieth Century Great House|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f5kwAQAAIAAJ|year=2002|publisher=Department for Continuing Education, Oxford University|isbn=978-0-903736-31-2|page=93}}</ref> but the park remains in private ownership.<ref name="englishheritage">{{cite web|title=At Risk Register 2012 (South East)|author=English Heritage|date=2013|access-date=15 September 2016|page=81|url=http://docplayer.net/45100197-Contents-heritage-at-risk-3-reducing-the-risks-7-publications-and-guidance-10-the-register-12-content-and-assessment-criteria-key-to-the-entries.html}}</ref> Some of the house's contents have also been acquired by the Trust in lieu of [[estate duty]].<ref>{{Cite Hansard |jurisdiction=United Kingdom |house=House of Commons |title=Works of Art (Taxation)|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/written-answers/1984/jul/06/works-of-art-taxation#column_341w |date=6 July 1984 |volume=63 |column=341W }}</ref>

Construction of the house, designed by Italian architect [[Giacomo Leoni]], began about 1730, and the interiors were finished by continental sculptors and plasterers in the 1740s. It replaced an [[Elizabethan]] house. The park was landscaped by [[Lancelot 'Capability' Brown]] in 1781, and there are two formal gardens on either side of the house. On the Epsom Road, leading to the park and house, are the Grade II* 18th century [[wrought iron]] gates with armorial [[Overthrow (structure)|overthrow]], which Brown installed, and the [[gatehouse]]s (1776), designed by Brown himself.<ref name="NHLE1188805">{{NHLE| num=1188805 |desc=Lodges and gates to Clandon Park House |grade=II* |accessdate=29 October 2021}}</ref>

Near the house is a [[Wharenui|Māori meeting house]], one of only four outside New Zealand, that was brought to England in the late 19th century. After being transferred to the National Trust, the house underwent restoration before it was opened to the public, and later became a wedding venue and filming location for period dramas.

Clandon Park House was badly damaged by fire in April 2015, probably caused by an electrical fault in the basement, leaving it "essentially a shell". Only one room, the Speaker's Parlour, was left intact. Thousands of historic artefacts, paintings, and items of furniture were lost in what has been described as a national tragedy.<ref name="furness" /> In January 2016, the National Trust announced that some of the principal rooms on the ground floor would be fully restored to the original 18th-century designs, and upper floors will be used for exhibitions and events.<!--cited in article body--> However, the Trust announced in 2022 its intention to restore only the Speaker's Parlour, the exterior walls, the roof and the windows and conserve the rest of the house in its ruined state while making it accessible to the public.<ref name="design for house">{{cite news |title=Clandon Park: National Trust reveals 'laid-bare' design for fire-hit house |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-surrey-62051843 |access-date=6 September 2023 |work=BBC News |date=6 July 2022}}</ref><ref name="The project at Clandon Park">{{cite web |title=The project at Clandon Park |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/surrey/clandon-park/the-project-at-clandon-park |website=National Trust |access-date=6 September 2023}}</ref> Building work is due to start in autumn 2025 and the property expected to reopen in 2029.<ref name=BBC25/>

==History==
The estate and [[Elizabethan]] house, together with Temple Court Farm at [[Merrow, Surrey|Merrow]], was purchased in 1641 from Sir [[Richard Weston (canal builder)|Richard Weston]] of nearby [[Sutton Place, Surrey|Sutton Place]],<ref>Harrison, pp. 121, 133.</ref> by [[Richard Onslow (Parliamentarian)|Sir Richard Onslow]], MP for Surrey in the [[Long Parliament]] and great-grandfather of [[Thomas Onslow, 2nd Baron Onslow]], who rebuilt it. Many members of the Onslow family followed political careers; three of them, including [[Arthur Onslow]], were [[Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)|Speakers]] of the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]]. Their portraits would later hang in the Speaker's Parlour at Clandon House.<ref name="Mason1979">{{cite book|author=Oliver Mason|title=South-east England|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Df15AAAAIAAJ|year=1979|publisher=J. Bartholomew|isbn=978-0-7028-1019-0|page=80}}</ref>

[[File:Clandon House 1824 engraving.jpg|thumb|Engraving of the house, showing the west front and deer park, c. 1824]]
The house was built, or perhaps thoroughly rebuilt, in about 1730–33 (the latter date is on rainwater heads) by [[Thomas Onslow, 2nd Baron Onslow]] to the design of the Venetian architect [[Giacomo Leoni]]. It is a rectangular building of red brick and stone dressings. Clandon House interiors, completed in the 1740s, featured a two-storey Marble Hall, containing marble chimney pieces by the Flemish sculptor [[Michael Rysbrack]], and a [[rococo]] plasterwork ceiling by Italian-Swiss artists [[Giuseppe Artari]] and Bagutti.<ref name=greeveshsitandland/>

Clandon Park was landscaped by [[Lancelot 'Capability' Brown]] in 1776–81, replacing a French garden and transforming part of a disused canal into an ornamental lake.<ref name="Clifford1974">{{cite book|author=Joan Clifford|title=Capability Brown: An Illustrated Life of Lancelot Brown, 1716–1783|url=https://archive.org/details/capabilitybrowni0000clif|url-access=registration|year=1974|publisher=Shire Publications|isbn=978-0-85263-274-1|page=[https://archive.org/details/capabilitybrowni0000clif/page/38 38]}}</ref> A [[porte-cochère]] was added to the principal façade in 1876. A sunken [[Dutch garden]] was created by Frances, Countess of Onslow at the north front of the house in the late 19th century. In 1895, the house was investigated for paranormal activity by [[John Crichton-Stuart, 3rd Marquess of Bute]] and [[Ada Goodrich Freer]] on behalf of the [[Society for Psychical Research]]. During [[World War I]], the Onslow family created and managed a hospital in Clandon House for the war injured.<ref>{{cite web|title=History|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/clandon-park/history/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 May 2015}}</ref>

===Slavery===
The house has been described as having been built partly with the profits from [[middle passage|slavery]]. In 1706, Elizabeth Knight inherited wealth equivalent to around £4 million from her uncle, Charles Knight, a slave trader and [[Sugar plantations in the Caribbean|plantation]] owner. This included a plantation in Jamaica where up to 150 enslaved workers produced sugar and rum. In 1708, Elizabeth married Thomas Onslow, the founder of an insurance company that dealt with [[slave ships]]. The plantation was subsequently passed down through the Onslow family. Enslaved people were freed after the [[Slavery Abolition Act 1833|Slavery Abolition Act]] was passed in the UK in 1833.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/clandon-park/features/clandon-park-a-house-built-on-the-profits-of-slavery|title=Clandon Park: A house built on the profits of slavery|website=National Trust|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220806164325/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/clandon-park/features/clandon-park-a-house-built-on-the-profits-of-slavery|archive-date=6 August 2022}}</ref>

===Acquisition by the National Trust===
In 1945, ownership of Clandon House was passed in trust to [[William Onslow, 6th Earl of Onslow]] on the death of his father, who had offered Clandon House to be used by the [[Public Record Office]] to protect government documents from destruction by bombs in the war. The family moved out to facilitate this. In 1956, the Earl decided that he wished to donate Clandon House to the nation. The house could not be donated directly by the Onslows, so the Earl arranged for his aunt, [[Gwendolen Guinness, Countess of Iveagh|Gwendolen, Countess Iveagh]], the daughter of [[William Hillier, 4th Earl of Onslow]] and a former MP herself, to purchase Clandon House from the Onslows for £1. The National Trust would only accept the house if it also received a substantial monetary endowment. This was arranged, and Clandon House with seven acres of land – including Hinemihi – were donated to the National Trust.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Dunton|first1=Jim|title=Fire ravages grade I-listed Surrey mansion|date=30 April 2015 |url=http://www.architectsjournal.co.uk/news/fire-ravages-grade-i-listed-surrey-mansion/8682234.article|publisher=Architects Journal|access-date=1 May 2015}}</ref><ref>''[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/cymraeg/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-clandonpark/w-clandonpark-maori-house/w-clandonpark-maori-house-4.htm Hinemihi at Clandon Park]'', National Trust, accessed 20 May 2010. {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629101422/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/cymraeg/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-clandonpark/w-clandonpark-maori-house/w-clandonpark-maori-house-4.htm |date=29 June 2011 }}</ref>

Historian [[James Lees-Milne]] described the house in 1942 as "dirty and in decay", and [[Merlin Waterson]], former director of historic properties at the National Trust, said it was "much depleted when it came to the Trust". Its state rooms were almost empty, but as well as many paintings and items of furniture belonging to the Onslow family, the house also contained some 18th-century porcelain, textiles and furniture donated by Hannah Gubbay, a member of the [[Sassoon family]].<ref name="ponsonby">{{cite book|author=Margaret Ponsonby|title=Faded and Threadbare: Historic Textiles and Their Role in Houses Open to the Public|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2TsHDAAAQBAJ|year=2016|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-317-13690-3|pages=34–36}}</ref>

===1968 – 2014===
It was extensively restored and redecorated between 1968 and 1970 by the interior designer [[John Beresford Fowler|John Fowler]], who set out to "capture the spirit of the rooms and its period rather than to replicate exact historical detail". Other pieces were acquired from the National Trust's extensive collections, and notable antiques that had a long-standing association with the property were also bought for display in the house. Many historians have criticised Fowler's design choices at Clandon House. Merlin Waterson admits "he was not given clear enough guidance on what was historically appropriate". However, [[Neil Cossons]], a historian and museum director, has said "[Fowler] was ever anxious to avoid the 'dead hand of the restorer'. In these interiors nothing jarred and they were completely in keeping with the romantic taste of the period".<ref name="ponsonby"/> In 1978, a [[parterre]] designed by John Fowler and Paul Miles was laid out on the south front, replacing early 20th-century flower beds.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1001171|desc=Clandon Park|accessdate=22 June 2018}}</ref>

By the 2000s, the house contained, among other things, the Ivo Forde [[Meissen]] collection of Italian comedy figures,<ref>{{cite web|title=Ceramics at Clandon Park|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1356396342649/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130310210610/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1356396342649/|archive-date=10 March 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Mortlake Tapestry Works|Mortlake tapestries]], and other rich textiles and carpets. Due to its extensive costs of upkeep, the National Trust gained a [[marriage licence]] for the property, and it had become a popular local wedding venue. It was also in part or whole rented out occasionally to the media for various productions, including 2008's ''[[The Duchess (film)|The Duchess]]'' starring [[Keira Knightley]].<ref>{{cite news|title=When Keira Knightley came to Clandon Park|url=http://www.surreylife.co.uk/out-about/when_keira_knightley_came_to_clandon_park_1_1632456|access-date=1 May 2015|work=Surrey Life|date=21 September 2012}}</ref>

In their 2012 At Risk Register, [[English Heritage]] described the park still owned by the Earl of Onslow as highly vulnerable, with extensive significant problems, and "unsympathetically managed thus affecting the overall integrity of the design and the setting of the house". Discussions about the development of a proposed [[business park]] were ongoing.<ref name="englishheritage"/>

===2015 fire===
[[File:Clandon House fire.jpg|thumb|House on fire in April 2015]]
On the afternoon of 29 April 2015, a fire started in the house's basement and quickly spread to the roof.<ref name=BBC32524445/> At 16:09, [[Surrey Fire and Rescue Service]] received an emergency call, and the fire was subsequently attended by a total of 16 fire engines and more than 80 personnel.<ref name=BBC32524445/> While fire fighters tackled the blaze, National Trust volunteers were joined by conservators in salvaging furniture and works of art,<ref name=BBC32524445/> with around 600 "significant items" rescued.<ref name=":0">Beer, H. (2018). Rising from the ashes. ''National Trust Magazine'', ''145''(Autumn), 29-32.</ref> The fire and rescue service remained at the property for a further ten days until the fire had been fully extinguished and then began an investigation into the cause of the fire.<ref name=BBC32524445>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-surrey-32524445 |title=Clandon Park House in Surrey hit by major fire |date=29 April 2015 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181028183126/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-surrey-32524445 |archive-date=28 October 2018 |url-status=dead |access-date=21 June 2018 }}</ref><ref name="GS-9148162">{{cite news |url=http://www.getsurrey.co.uk/news/local-news/clandon-park-fire-massive-amount-9148162 |last=Stubbings |first=David |date=29 April 2015 |title=Clandon Park fire: 'Massive' amount of smoke seen from 18th century house |publisher=[[Trinity Mirror]] Southern |work=Get Surrey website |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150501175733/http://www.getsurrey.co.uk/news/local-news/clandon-park-fire-massive-amount-9148162 |archive-date=1 May 2015 |url-status=dead |access-date=29 April 2015 }}</ref><ref name=":0" />

Although a significant number of items were salvaged, the house was left "essentially a shell" according to Dame [[Helen Ghosh]], director general of the National Trust.<ref name=GuardClandonShell>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2015/apr/30/clandon-park-fire-leaves-surrey-stately-home-essentially-a-shell|title=Clandon Park fire leaves Surrey stately home 'essentially a shell'|work=The Guardian|date=30 April 2015 |access-date=30 April 2015}}</ref> The roof, ceilings and floors had fallen into the basement, leaving just one room intact.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-surrey-32528435 |title= Clandon Park House fire: Mansion left a 'shell'|work= BBC News|date= 30 April 2015|publisher=BBC|access-date=30 April 2015}}</ref> One of the footballs kicked across no-man's land on the first day of the [[Battle of the Somme]] in 1916 was among the thousands of historic items destroyed, but the six [[Victoria Cross]]es thought to have been destroyed were replicas – the originals were held in a bank vault.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/11573006/Clandon-House-salvage-operation-after-huge-stately-home-fire.html|title= Clandon Park left as a 'shell' after huge stately home fire|newspaper=Daily Telegraph|access-date=1 May 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vconline.org.uk/queens-royal-surrey-regiment/4588870711|title=Queens Royal Surrey Regiment Museum, Clanford Park, Surrey|work=VCs and GCs Online|access-date=6 December 2017}}</ref> Although some paintings and furniture were rescued by staff, many tapestries and some items of porcelain were heavily damaged.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Davies|first1=Caroline|title=Clandon Park salvage operation under way after fire rips through stately home|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2015/apr/30/clandon-park-house-fire-salvage-stately-home-surrey|access-date=1 May 2015|work=Guardian|date=30 April 2015}}</ref> A large portrait of [[Richard Onslow, 1st Baron Onslow]] who was [[Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)|Speaker of the House of Commons]] in the early 18th century, was saved after being cut from its frame.<ref name=":1">{{cite news|last=Singh |first=Anita |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/11574829/Battle-of-the-Somme-football-among-priceless-artifacts-lost-in-Clandon-House-blaze.html |title=Battle of the Somme football among priceless artifacts lost in Clandon Park blaze |newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |date=30 April 2015 |access-date=1 May 2015}}</ref> Among the items workers prioritised to rescue were the regimental colours.<ref name=":1" /> An official investigation concluded that the fire was probably caused by a fault on an electrical distribution board in the basement.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/12018812/Clandon-Park-mansion-fire-caused-by-fuse-board-fault-investigation-finds.html|title=Clandon Park mansion fire caused by fuse board fault, investigation finds|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=26 November 2015|access-date=18 January 2016}}</ref>

==Restoration project==
[[File:Clandon House ruins.jpg|thumb|Burnt-out shell of Clandon Park]]
In January 2016, the National Trust announced that a number of the principal rooms were going to be restored to the original 18th-century designs, and the "less architecturally significant" upper floors were to be fully modernised for holding exhibitions, events and performances.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-surrey-35343464|title=Clandon Park House to be partly restored after fire|work=BBC News |date=18 January 2016 |access-date=18 January 2016}}</ref> The cost of the restoration work is being funded by an insurance payout estimated at £65 million.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://theartnewspaper.com/news/news/national-trust-to-restore-fire-devastated-clandon-park-/|title=National Trust to restore fire-devastated Clandon Park|author=Martin Bailey|date=18 January 2016|access-date=18 January 2016|newspaper=The Art Newspaper}}</ref> A spokesman for the trust said it would also be asking supporters for donations to cover any shortfall in the budget.<ref name="furness"/>

[[Rupert Onslow, 8th Earl of Onslow]] who owns and manages <!--the 1000 acre ?? lead says "220-hectare (540-acre)"? --> Clandon Park, whose family were the last private owners of Clandon House, criticised the decision to build "a replica" of the house, saying the money might be better spent on adding properties in need of genuine conservation to the National Trust's collection. The Earl said, "Clandon is lost. It's a ruin now. It decayed instantly. If the National Trust wants a replica, let them build it somewhere else." He also said that the last thing he wanted was a "Vulgar [[mock-Georgian]] footballers' wives house." However, the trust said the insurance policy did not allow it to spend the money elsewhere, and it could only be spent at Clandon. The [[Georgian Group]] welcomed the decision, calling the fire a national tragedy, and lending support for the restoration project,<ref name="furness">{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/12105182/Clandon-Park-fire-National-Trust-to-restore-stately-home.html|title=Clandon Park fire: National Trust to restore stately home in 'biggest project in a generation'|newspaper=The Telegraph|author=Hannah Furness|date=18 January 2016|access-date=18 January 2016}}</ref> but reversed its position in September 2017 when the shortlist of design teams being considered for the restoration, and their initial proposals, were revealed.<ref name="hope">{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/09/09/national-trust-now-embarrassed-elite-houses-georgian-group-says/|title=National Trust is now too embarrassed to own 'elite houses', Georgian Group says, in furious attack on Clandon Park plans|newspaper=The Telegraph|author=Christopher Hope|date=9 September 2017|access-date=17 September 2017}}</ref>

In December 2017, architects [[Allies and Morrison]] were unanimously chosen as the winner of an international design competition to restore Clandon Park House.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://competitions.malcolmreading.co.uk/clandonpark/news|title=Allies and Morrison wins international design competition to restore, reimagine and rebuild Clandon Park|publisher=Malcolm Reading Consultants|access-date=27 January 2018}}</ref>

In 2022, the Trust announced its intention to drop the previously announced restoration project on account of few original features surviving, in favour of only restoring the Speaker's Parlour (the only room to survive the fire intact) and the external walls and the windows, while the exterior of the building would appear as it did before the blaze. The inside of the house would be conserved in its ruined state and made accessible to the public by installing new walkways to provide a unique insight into the construction of an 18th-century stately home. The Trust also plans to add a new rooftop terrace, offering views of the surrounding countryside.<ref name="design for house" /><ref name="The project at Clandon Park" /> The plans were approved by [[Guildford Borough Council]], and building work is expected to start in autumn 2025 and be completed by 2029.<ref name=BBC25>{{cite news |title=Stately home to be part-restored after large fire|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c757q6xrv7yo |access-date=28 March 2025|work=BBC News |date=7 March 2025}}</ref>

==Maori meeting house==
[[Image:MaoriMeetingHouse-ClandonPark.JPG|thumb|Hinemihi, the [[Māori people|Māori]] meeting house]]
A [[Māori people|Māori]] meeting house or [[wharenui]] named ''Hinemihi'' stands in the gardens. It was originally situated near [[Lake Tarawera]] in [[New Zealand]] and provided shelter to the people of [[Te Wairoa (village)|Te Wairoa]] village during the eruption of [[Mount Tarawera]] in 1886. The building was covered in ash and surrounded by volcanic debris, but its occupants survived. It remained half buried until 1892 when [[William Onslow, 4th Earl of Onslow]], then [[Governor General of New Zealand]], bought it and had it fully restored and shipped to England.<ref name=greeveshsitandland>{{cite book|last1=Greeves|first1=Lydia|title=History and Landscape: The Guide to National Trust Properties in England, Wales and Northern Ireland|date=2006|publisher=National Trust Books|isbn=978-1905400133|pages=94–95}}</ref> There are only three other Māori meeting houses outside New Zealand.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gardens-to-go.org.uk/clandon_park.htm|title=Clandon Park|work=gardens-to-go.org.uk|access-date=30 April 2015}}</ref>

The National Trust has refurbished the Maori meeting house,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/clandon-park/things-to-see-and-do/maori-meeting-house/|title=Maori meeting house|access-date=15 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150912223943/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/clandon-park/things-to-see-and-do/maori-meeting-house/|archive-date=12 September 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> replacing the roof, cleaning and repainting carvings, and replacing carvings that were lost. The roof is thatched, based on a misinterpretation of a photograph of the house covered in ash. Its original roof was of shingles.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aucklandartgallery.com/explore-art-and-ideas/artwork/21637/hinemihi-clandon-house-surrey-united-kingdom-2000|title=Hinemihi, Clandon House, Surrey, United Kingdom 2000|website=Auckland Art Gallery|access-date=15 April 2019}}</ref> The [[Heritage New Zealand|New Zealand Historic Places Trust]] and the [[British Museum]] were consulted over this work. The meeting house is still important for cultural activities among the Māori.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.exploringsurreyspast.org.uk/themes/places/surrey/guildford/west_clandon/west_clandon_clandon_park_himenihi_the_maori_meeting_house/|title=West Clandon: The Maori meeting house (Hinemihi) – Clandon Park — Exploring Surrey's Past|work=exploringsurreyspast.org.uk|access-date=30 April 2015}}</ref> The nature of Hinemihi and its meaning for the local and expatriate Maori community in London was explored by Cecilie Gravesen in her experimental film ''Between Humans and Other Things'' (2010).<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Gravesen | first1 = C | year = 2012 | title = Between Humans and Other Things: Conservation as Material Fabric in Contemporary Art | url =http://www.jcms-journal.com/article/view/jcms.1011201 | journal = Journal of Conservation and Museum Studies | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | doi = 10.5334/jcms.1011201 | doi-access = free }}</ref> During the [[2012 Summer Olympics]], the New Zealand team visited Hinemihi.<ref>{{cite news|title=New Zealand Olympic team visits Surrey Maori meeting house|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-surrey-19192852|work=BBC News|access-date=1 May 2015}}</ref>

==Surrey Infantry Museum==
{{Main|Surrey Infantry Museum}}
Colonel JW Sewell reached agreement with the National Trust to re-establish the Queen's Royal Surrey Regiment Museum at Clandon House. The museum opened in 1981 with exhibits including uniforms, medals, weapons, regalia, photographs and memorabilia. The regiment's archives and library are located at the [[Surrey History Centre]] in [[Woking]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.surreycc.gov.uk/recreation-heritage-and-culture/archives-and-history/surrey-history-centre/highlights-of-our-holdings-at-surrey-history-centre/the-queens-royal-surrey-regiment |title=The Queen's Royal Surrey Regiment |publisher=Surrey History Centre |access-date=9 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120117073440/http://www.surreycc.gov.uk/recreation-heritage-and-culture/archives-and-history/surrey-history-centre/highlights-of-our-holdings-at-surrey-history-centre/the-queens-royal-surrey-regiment |archive-date=17 January 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> After being upgraded in 2001, in July 2011 with part funding from the [[Heritage Lottery Fund]] the museum merged with those of the [[Princess of Wales's Royal Regiment]] and the [[Queen's Royal Surrey Regiment]] to become the Surrey Infantry Museum.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.queensroyalsurreys.org.uk/new_museum/new_museum.shtml |title=Surrey Infantry Museum at Clandon Park |publisher=The Queen's Royal Surrey Regimental Association |access-date=22 October 2012}}</ref> The museum's displayed medal collection included six [[Victoria Cross]]es, including those awarded to: Lieutenant [[Wallace Duffield Wright]]; Lance Corporal [[Leonard James Keyworth]]; Corporal [[John McNamara (VC)|John McNamara]]; Second Lieutenant [[Arthur James Terence Fleming-Sandes]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.victoriacross.org.uk/ccqrosur.htm|title=Surrey Infantry Museum|publisher=Victoria Cross|access-date=22 June 2018}}</ref> The museum, housed in the basement, was totally destroyed in the fire.

'''Claremont Landscape Garden''', just outside [[Esher]], [[Surrey]], [[England]], is one of the earliest surviving gardens of its kind of [[landscape design]], the [[English garden|English Landscape Garden]] — still featuring its original 18th-century layout. The garden is Grade I listed on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|num=1000324|desc=Claremont|access-date=10 February 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref> 

==History==
Originally created for [[Claremont (country house)|Claremont House]], it represents the work of some of the best known [[landscape gardener]]s, such as [[Charles Bridgeman]], [[Capability Brown]], [[William Kent]] and Sir [[John Vanbrugh]].

Work on the gardens began around 1715 and by 1727 they were described as "the noblest of any in Europe".{{cn|date=December 2019}} Within the grounds, overlooking the lake, is an unusual-turfed amphitheatre, which used to form the centrepiece of an annual event called the Claremont [[Fête champêtre]]. Hundreds of visitors descended on Claremont, most in costume (each year has a different theme) to enjoy four days of music, theatre and fireworks.

==Stewardship==
Also within the grounds is the Belvedere Tower, designed by Sir John Vanbrugh for the [[Thomas Pelham-Holles, 1st Duke of Newcastle-upon-Tyne|Duke of Newcastle]]. The tower is unusual in that what appear to be windows, are actually [[Trompe-l'œil|bricks painted black and white]].  It is now owned by [[Claremont (country house)#Claremont Fan Court School|Claremont Fan Court School]], which is situated alongside the gardens.

In 1949 the landscape garden was donated to the [[National Trust]] for stewardship and protection. Initially it was managed by [[Esher Urban District|Esher Urban District Council]], who could do little more than basic maintenance and grass-cutting.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home Landscaping and Garden Fair |url=https://heritagedrivesandlandscapes.co.uk/ |access-date=2023-03-15 |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1974, the National Trust took back control of the site and a pioneering restoration programme was launched in 1975 following a significant donation by the Slater Foundation.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Chessum |first1=Sophie |title=Claremont |last2=Rogers |first2=Kevin |last3=Rowell |first3=Christopher |date=2000 |publisher=National Trust |location=Swindon |page=20, 55}}</ref>

==Transport==
The entrance to the garden is directly off the [[A307 road|A307, Portsmouth Road]]. Buses from Kingston on Thames, Esher and Guildford stop nearby. The road originally ran closer to the lake but [[Robert Clive]] had it moved further north to its present alignment in 1771.<ref name=":0" />

2320167.title: Hatchlands Park
2320167.extract: Hatchlands Park is a red-brick country house with surrounding gardens in East Clandon, Surrey, England, covering 170 hectares (430 acres). It is located near Guildford along the A246 between East Clandon and West Horsley. Hatchlands Park has been a Grade I listed property since 1967. The gardens were Grade II listed in 2007.

'''Hatchlands Park''' is a red-brick [[country house]] with surrounding gardens in [[East Clandon]], [[Surrey]], [[England]], covering 170 hectares (430 acres). It is located near [[Guildford]] along the A246 between East Clandon and [[West Horsley]]. Hatchlands Park has been a Grade I listed property since 1967.<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|num=1294970|desc=Hatchlands|access-date=8 November 2017|mode=cs2}}</ref> The gardens were Grade II listed in 2007.<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Hatchlands|num=1001697|access-date=22 March 2019}}</ref>

==History==
The park initially belonged to the [[Chertsey Abbey]] with the park being mentioned in the [[Domesday Book]]. In 1544, after the [[dissolution of the monasteries]], it was granted by [[Henry VIII]] to Sir Anthony Browne and his wife, Lady [[Elizabeth FitzGerald, Countess of Lincoln|Elizabeth Fitzgerald]] ('The Fair Geraldine' of [[Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey|Henry Howard]]).<ref name=nt>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-hatchlandspark/w-hatchlandspark-history.htm National Trust ''Hatchlands history''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080708221814/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-hatchlandspark/w-hatchlandspark-history.htm |date=2008-07-08 }}</ref> The first visual record of the park is shown on a [[John Seller]] map of 1693.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.crouchrarebooks.com/maps/view/seller-john-surrey-actually-surveyd-and-delineated1|title=Surrey - John Seller's rare map of Surrey|year=1700|publisher=Daniel Crouch Rare Books|access-date=29 July 2018|archive-date=29 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180729230534/http://www.crouchrarebooks.com/maps/view/seller-john-surrey-actually-surveyd-and-delineated1|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The park was purchased in 1750 by Admiral [[Edward Boscawen]] who landscaped the grounds; for the house he employed the architect [[Stiff Leadbetter]], with [[Robert Adam]] designing some interiors. Edward Boscawen's widow, Fanny sold the estate in 1770 to the Sumner family of the [[East India Company]]; both father and son made further alterations to the property.<ref name=NHLE/> The father, William Brightwell Sumner commissioned Benjamin Armitage to make alterations, and his son, George Holme Sumner asked [[Humphry Repton]] (1752–1818) to redesign the park and garden.<ref name=NHLE/> Towards the end of the century, [[Joseph Bonomi the Elder]] was commissioned to alter several rooms and to impose a frontispiece on the west front.<ref name=NHLE/>

In 1888, the Sumner family sold the estate to Stuart Rendel, later [[Stuart Rendel, 1st Baron Rendel|Lord Rendel]].<ref name=NHLE/> He had extensive changes made to the fabric of the house. Rendel was mainly his own architect but he also employed his nephew by marriage, Halsey Ricardo, and commissioned [[Reginald Blomfield]] to build the Music Room. Rendel coloured and gilded Robert Adam's ceilings, embellished the staircase with rococo decorations and switched the main entrance of the house to the east.  Rendel also commissioned [[Gertrude Jekyll]] to design the gardens which contain a [[parterre]].<ref>[http://freespace.virgin.net/martin.farncombe/gardens/gardenhtm/page42.htm The gardens by Judy Farncombe] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070421203317/http://freespace.virgin.net/martin.farncombe/gardens/gardenhtm/page42.htm |date=2007-04-21 }} retrieved 21/4/07</ref><ref name=NHLE/> Lord Rendel's grandson, [[Harry Stuart Goodhart-Rendel]], who was an architect and [[British Army]] officer, inherited the house in 1913.<ref name=NHLE/> He passed the estate to the [[National Trust]] in 1945.<ref name=NHLE/>

The house is open to the public, but closed on certain days of the week. However, the parkland is now open 363 days a year. There is a café and a shop. There is a [[Cobblestone|cobbled]] courtyard.<ref>[http://www.guildford.gov.uk/GuildfordWeb/Tourism/Groups/HatchlandsPark.htm Guildford Borough Council] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927233601/http://www.guildford.gov.uk/GuildfordWeb/Tourism/Groups/HatchlandsPark.htm |date=2007-09-27 }}</ref>

==The interior==
The house contains splendid interiors by Robert Adam, decorated in appropriately nautical style: anchors, cannon, dolphins and sea-nymphs are presided over by Neptune himself run through the house reflecting its first owner Edward Boscawen.<ref name=nt/>

==Cobbe Collection==
[[File:Cobbe portrait of Shakespeare.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Cobbe portrait]], possibly of [[William Shakespeare]]]]
The house is home to the [[Cobbe family|Cobbe]] Collection; with forty two historic [[keyboard instrument]]s it is the world's largest group of its kind.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cecilia-uk.org/html/search/verb/GetRecord/824 |title=Cobbe Collection of keyboard instruments |publisher=Cecilia |access-date=29 July 2018 |archive-date=29 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180729230538/http://www.cecilia-uk.org/html/search/verb/GetRecord/824/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Many of the instruments are associated with famous composers. The instruments include [[harpsichord]]s and [[fortepiano]]s dating from 1750 to 1840 – including an Erard pianoforte reputedly made for [[Marie Antoinette]]. It is one of the few French instruments of the time to escape destruction for firewood following the 1789 [[French Revolution]]. The pieces were brought together to represent those instrument makers who were highly regarded or patronised by composers, rather than to illustrate a complete or technical history of keyboard manufacture. Twelve of the instruments were actually owned or played by great composers such as [[Henry Purcell|Purcell]], [[J. C. Bach]], [[Mozart]], [[Beethoven]], [[Chopin]], [[Liszt]], [[Gustav Mahler|Mahler]] and [[Elgar]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/hatchlands-park/lists/the-cobbe-collection-at-hatchlands-park|title=Cobbe Collection|publisher=National Trust|access-date=29 July 2018}}</ref>

Hatchlands also houses part of the Cobbe collection of paintings, including what is claimed to be one of only two surviving [[Cobbe portrait|portraits]] of [[William Shakespeare]] painted during his lifetime.<ref>{{cite book |title=Hatchlands Park - List of the Cobbe collection of paintings |publisher=National Trust |location=Swindon |page=1}}</ref>

A group of dwellings known as the Isle of Wight is situated within the site, and a track, Common Road, leads to it from the northwest. Little Bookham Common (the smaller of the two parts of the site) lies south and west of this track, whereas Great Bookham Common lies to the east.
Together the two commons comprise a Site of Special Scientific Interest.
The site is owned by the National Trust. A network of public footpaths and public bridleways cross the site: in addition, there are a number of concessionary horse rides.

'''Bookham Commons'''  are two [[common land|commons]], situated just to the north of the villages of [[Great Bookham]] and [[Little Bookham]], in [[Surrey]], [[England]], {{convert|154.7|ha|acre|abbr=off}} in extent; the individual parts are named '''Great Bookham Common''' and '''Little Bookham Common'''. A group of dwellings known as the Isle of Wight is situated within the site, and a track, Common Road, leads to it from the northwest. Little Bookham Common (the smaller of the two parts of the site) lies south and west of this track, whereas Great Bookham Common lies to the east.

Together the two commons comprise a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]].

The site is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]. A network of [[Rights of way in England and Wales|public footpaths]] and public bridleways cross the site: in addition, there are a number of concessionary horse rides.<ref name=NationalTrust />

== Site description ==
The site sits on [[London Clay]]. [[Habitat (ecology)|Habitat]] types present include [[woodland]], [[scrubland|scrub]], [[grassland]] and open water.

Woodland covers approximately two-thirds of the site. The majority of this woodland is mature and dominated by [[pedunculate oak]] (''Quercus robur''). These woodlands are dissected by a network of rides.

Little Bookham Common is a mosaic of rough grassland and scrub; much of this common is poorly drained and there are several old [[gunpit]]s and [[bomb crater]]s. The areas of open grassland are dominated by [[tufted hair-grass]] (''Deschampsia cespitosa'').

There are several woodland [[pond]]s on the site and a [[tributary]] of the [[River Mole, Surrey|River Mole]] runs across it.

== Biodiversity interest ==
{{unsourced|section|date=July 2025}}
The site's nature conservation importance (the reason for SSSI designation), is due to its plant communities, its community of breeding birds and its invertebrate communities.

[[Thin-spiked wood sedge]] (''Carex strigosa''), which is scarce in Surrey, is present in woodlands at the site. Two species of rose which are scarce in Surrey, ''[[Rosa micrantha]]'' and ''[[Rosa stylosa]]'' are found in the scrub on Little Bookham Common. The [[bryophyte]] flora in the site's woodland is rich and includes one of only two Surrey localities for the moss ''[[Zygodon conoideus]]''. Notable plants found in the grassland of Little Bookham Common include [[southern marsh-orchid]] (''Dactylorhiza praetermissa''), [[pepper-saxifrage]] (''Silaum silaus''), [[spiked sedge]] (''Carex spicata'') and [[Ophioglossum vulgatum|adder’s-tongue fern]] (''Ophioglossum vulgatum''). The flora of the site's open water habitats includes three plants which are scarce in Surrey: [[greater duckweed]] (''Lemna polyrhiza''), [[fat duckweed]] (''Lemna gibba'') and [[thread-leaved water-crowfoot]] (''Ranunculus trichophyllus''), while [[tall-herb fen]] communities here support two plants which are rare in Surrey, the grass [[orange foxtail]] (''Alopecurus aequalis'') and [[eared willow]] (''Salix aurita'').

Breeding birds which are associated with woodland at this site include [[hawfinch]], [[woodcock]] and [[lesser spotted woodpecker]], whilst those breeding in scrub areas include [[nightingale]] and [[grasshopper warbler]].

The site has a very well-recorded invertebrate fauna, which includes 611 species of [[beetle]], 1140 species of [[Diptera|fly]], 146 [[Hemiptera|true bugs]], 201 [[spider]]s, 17 [[dragonfly|dragonflies]] and over 300 species of butterflies and moths.

Dead oak trees provide habitat for several beetles which are scarce in Surrey including ''[[Nemadus colonoides]]'' and ''[[Aridius nodifer]]''. Two moths which occur, the [[Calophasia lunula|toadflax brocade]] and the [[Hemaris fuciformis|broad-bordered bee hawkmoth]] are [[nationally rare]]. This is a well-known site for the [[Apatura iris|purple emperor]], and other scarce butterflies which are present include [[white-letter hairstreak|white-letter]] and [[purple hairstreak]]s and the [[Limenitis camilla|white admiral]].

10462680.extract:
Dapdune Wharf is a former industrial wharf and boat yard on the Wey and Godalming Navigations in Guildford, England, UK, close to the Surrey County Cricket Club ground. It is now maintained by the National Trust.
Originally a goods transshipment point, before the construction of the Godalming Navigation the principal cargos were timber from the Surrey forests and gunpowder from the works at Chilworth, as the Guildford authorities refused to let it pass through the town centre for loading at the town wharf. For a period of time at the beginning of the 20th Century, Dapdune Wharf was the centre of barge building on the Wey Navigation.
Dapdune is now the starting point for boat trips, including boat hire. The Visitor Centre has interactive displays, a smithy, a stable, and two of the three remaining Wey barges in the world - the Reliance, permanently damaged and kept in a graving (dry) dock, and Perseverance IV, still floating but in need of repair and the subject of a 2010 National Trust restoration appeal.
Dapdune Wharf is now the head office of the Navigation.  As part of the continued preservation of British history the National Trust has a group of volunteers, the Wey Navigation Research Group, researching and publishing information about the Godalming and Wey Navigation.
